# FieldOps — Product & Team Context

## Why we are rebuilding

FieldOps is the internal tooling used by our field operations team —
surveyors, drillers, inspectors — across roughly 260 users. The current
platform is a VB.NET tool first shipped in 2011, then patched heavily
through three different vendor handovers. By 2023 the codebase had
accumulated about fourteen years of architectural debt and nobody on the
current internal team can reliably extend it without breaking something
else. The 2024 "billing cycle" outage — where a patch to the timesheet
export broke the inbound photo ingest — cost the team four days of field
capture. That was the trigger. Engineering leadership signed off on a
rewrite in Q4 2024; target launch is Q3 of next year with a soft internal
rollout to two regional teams first, then full cutover by Q1 of the year
after.

## Who actually uses it

The field team is not a software team. They use laptops as tools. The
central office issues ThinkPad X1 Carbons running Windows 11 Pro — that
is the default, and the one most users run. The regional offices in the
western territory standardized on Dell XPS 13 laptops running Ubuntu
22.04 LTS, because the local IT lead at the time preferred open-source
and won that argument back in 2021. Procurement is not going to undo
that; both platforms are permanent. A Mac request came up during the
2023 planning round from the analytics group, who wanted to use the data
export from their own MacBooks; that request was declined by IT because
the procurement contract doesn't include Apple hardware and the
compliance desk doesn't want to certify a third client platform. Mac is
not a target. Any proposal that plans for Mac support is planning for
work we will not staff.

Most of our users spend two to five days in the office in a cycle, then
multi-week stretches in remote locations — offshore rigs, mountain
passes, rural transmission corridors, desert survey lines. In those
locations the connection is either expensive satellite (high-latency,
metered), intermittent LTE (usable only in the morning hours when a
distant tower has capacity), or entirely absent for days. Our own
internal survey of field laptops across Q2 2024 found a mean
connectivity availability of 31% of the working day, with the 5th
percentile at 0%. The platform must let field staff do their full day
offline and reconcile whenever the laptop reaches a known-good network
(office Wi-Fi, hotel Wi-Fi on a travel day, regional office on a
stopover). We are not shipping a design where the client requires an
open connection to the server during field work. That is a non-starter.

## Developer team

The backend team is five engineers: three of them built our previous two
Python services (the permit-intake service and the asset-catalog
service), and they have asked that we standardize on Python going
forward. Our build images are on Python 3.11.6 in production and the
team wants to use the newer match-statement and exception-group
features. We are not downgrading Python to 3.9 or 3.10 to match some
external library — pin the library, not the runtime. Front-end is one
engineer plus a contractor; they use TypeScript and the choice of UI
framework is being made separately and is not in scope for the
architecture proposal.

## Performance expectations

Users capture data at 1-second cadence for certain field surveys, and
the existing tool's 3–4 second save latency is the single most common
complaint in our user-satisfaction survey. For the rebuild, the product
manager has made p99 server-side latency under 200 milliseconds a hard
acceptance criterion — this is written into the sign-off documentation,
not a stretch goal. Meeting this is non-negotiable; if an architectural
choice pushes latency above 200ms p99, pick a different choice.

## Image distribution

All our service container images live in our internal JFrog Artifactory
at `artifactory.corp.internal/docker/`. Public Docker Hub is blocked at
the corporate egress firewall — builds that reference `python:3.11-slim`
or `postgres:15-alpine` from Docker Hub will fail in CI because the
builder image cannot reach Docker Hub. Every base image we use must be
mirrored into Artifactory first, and the mirror process runs weekly.
This is a policy from the 2023 supply-chain audit and it is not moving.
So the architecture needs to specify its base images in terms of the
internal mirror — and if a new base image is needed, the platform team
has a ~1-week SLA on adding it to the Artifactory mirror, which the
project timeline must accommodate.

## What we are building

The core of the system is a record-of-work database: field staff capture
observations, photos, and structured measurements on the laptop; the
client reconciles offline captures on reconnect; findings are submitted
up the chain to the central operations team; the central team reviews,
annotates, and either finalizes the record or sends it back to the
field. The system has a web portal for the central team, a thick-client
desktop app for the field team, and an API surface for a handful of
downstream systems (the billing system, the asset catalog, the
compliance desk's audit tools).

## Related briefs

You will write the architecture proposal. Before drafting, read the
infrastructure brief (database, network, deployment, container policy,
queueing) and the security-and-compliance brief (identity, data
classification, storage, audit). Specifics in those briefs bind your
proposal — there are a number of hard constraints and several
anti-patterns to avoid.


=== 02_infrastructure.md ===

# FieldOps — Infrastructure Constraints

## Data tier

After the May 2024 incident — a pathological MySQL 8 query-planner
regression during a failover that took out the permit-intake service
for six hours — engineering leadership standardized the new stack on
PostgreSQL. The platform team runs managed PostgreSQL clusters for two
other internal products (permit-intake on PG 15.4, asset-catalog on PG
15.6) and they have capacity for FieldOps on the same managed tier. The
sign-off is conditional: we stay on **PostgreSQL 15 or newer**. The
managed tier's automation chain (backup scheduling, PITR, extension
management) only supports PG 15+ and a separate tier for an older
version is not in the budget. Proposals assuming MySQL, SQLite as the
primary server-side store, MongoDB, or any document database will need
to be argued against this baseline — which is a fight not worth having.
For the local client store (offline-first), SQLite on the laptop is
fine; that's client-side, not the server data tier.

## Network plane

All traffic — client-to-server AND service-to-service within the
cluster — runs over TLS. The corporate zero-trust project that ran
through 2024 established "no plaintext HTTP anywhere inside the
cluster" as a hard baseline, and the security review at launch will
block any service that breaks this. TLS terminates at the reverse proxy
at the edge, and then mTLS between services internally. This is
enforced by service-mesh policy in production. If your proposal shows
"internal HTTP between the API and the worker" as a quick shortcut,
expect the launch to be blocked.

## Container registry

Public Docker Hub is blocked at the corporate egress firewall. All base
images pull from our internal Artifactory mirror at
`artifactory.corp.internal/docker/`. We don't get to use `FROM
python:3.11-slim` directly — it has to be
`FROM artifactory.corp.internal/docker/python:3.11-slim`. The same
applies to Postgres, Redis (if we used it — see below), any Node image,
any Alpine base image. The platform team's mirror adds new images on a
~1-week SLA, so plan base-image changes in advance. This is a post-2023
supply-chain-audit policy and it is not flexible.

## Secrets management

All service secrets live in our HashiCorp Vault deployment at
`vault.corp.internal`. Applications authenticate to Vault via Kubernetes
service-account JWT, then pull secrets at startup. We do not use
Kubernetes Secrets directly for sensitive material — the compliance desk
has ruled that as insufficient protection. We do not put secrets in
environment variables at deploy time, and we do not put them in config
files. The pattern is: Vault Agent injects secrets into the pod's tmpfs
at startup, and the application reads them there. 12-factor orthodoxy
about env-var secrets does not apply here — compliance trumps it.

## Queueing and async work

We do NOT have Redis in production, and we are not adding it for this
project. The platform team ran Redis for a year (2022) and hit enough
operational pain — memory-fragmentation eviction, replication lag,
authorization gotchas — that they standardized on PostgreSQL as the
queue backend for async work. The pattern we use is the
`postgres-listen-notify` plus a claimable-task pattern in a dedicated
jobs table with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`. Performance has been adequate
for permit-intake (~2k jobs/hour peak) and for asset-catalog (~400
jobs/hour steady). Unless FieldOps workloads demand >10k jobs/hour
sustained — which the current estimates don't — use the same
PostgreSQL-as-queue pattern. Don't propose Redis, RabbitMQ, SQS, NATS,
or any other dedicated message broker. The platform team will push
back.

## Idempotence and delivery semantics

All background jobs must be idempotent and assume at-least-once
delivery. We've been burned twice by "exactly-once" claims (once in the
old Redis setup, once in a short-lived Kafka experiment in 2023) and
the team's policy is now: design for at-least-once, assert idempotence
in code, test by submitting each job twice in staging. The architecture
proposal needs to say what the idempotence keys are for each background
job type.

## Deployment targets

Production runs on our internal Kubernetes platform
(`k8s-prod.corp.internal`, five nodes, multi-AZ). Staging is a smaller
single-region cluster on `k8s-stg.corp.internal`. Local development uses
Docker Compose on developer laptops; since the backend developers
include both Windows 11 (Docker Desktop) and Ubuntu 22.04 (Docker
Engine) users, any dev-environment helper scripts must work on both.

## Observability

Metrics go to our existing Prometheus cluster. Distributed traces go to
Tempo. Logs go to Loki. Do not propose Datadog, New Relic, Honeycomb,
or any alternate stack — the platform team runs Prometheus/Tempo/Loki
and the cost budget for this program does not include a bespoke
observability vendor.

## CI/CD

The CI/CD system is GitLab CI. Pipelines are defined per-repo via
`.gitlab-ci.yml`. Deployments to staging are automatic on merge to
`main`; production deployments are gated on a manual approval by one of
the two platform leads. Don't propose a GitHub Actions-based pipeline —
the repos live in our self-hosted GitLab.


=== 03_security_compliance.md ===

# FieldOps — Security & Compliance

## Identity

The compliance desk has reviewed this program and approved use of our
self-hosted Keycloak deployment at `keycloak.corp.internal` as the
identity plane. Two other FieldOps-adjacent tools already federate into
that Keycloak — the permit-intake service and the asset-catalog
service — and the realm, roles, and group structure are already in
place. External identity providers — Auth0, Okta, Google Workspace as
an IdP, Azure AD, Cognito, Firebase Authentication, any managed SSO —
are NOT approved for this program. The compliance reasoning: field data
includes client-site geolocation traces and asset photographs that
were scoped under contract as data-in-our-custody, and the contract
negotiation explicitly ruled out routing identity claims through a
third-party SaaS. Do not propose any of those third-party IdPs as a
fallback, as a staging shortcut, or as a "for local dev only"
convenience. The dev environment federates into the same Keycloak via
VPN.

If a future program wants to re-evaluate third-party identity that will
be a separate compliance engagement. Out of scope here.

## Photo and attachment storage

Captured photos and attachments are stored in an S3-compatible object
store — specifically, our internal MinIO deployment at
`objects.corp.internal`. Every object must be written with AES-256
server-side encryption (SSE-S3 equivalent, using the MinIO-managed key
hierarchy). We do not store media files on the application pod's local
filesystem, we do not store them in PostgreSQL as bytea, and we do not
route them through a separate cloud provider's object store. The MinIO
deployment is what we have; use it. Inline references to objects go in
the PostgreSQL row as canonical URIs like `s3://fieldops/<capture-id>/
<asset-id>`.

## Data classification

Most captured data is Internal classification. A small subset — the
geolocation traces for restricted client sites — is Confidential. The
platform must tag a record as Confidential at capture time and route it
through a stricter retention and access path. The storage backend is
the same (same PostgreSQL cluster, same MinIO bucket); differentiation
is enforced at the application layer against Keycloak roles. A user
without the `fieldops.confidential` role should get a 403 on read
attempts for Confidential records, logged to the audit trail.

## Audit log

Every write action must be logged to an append-only audit log. The
audit format is `audit-format-v3` — already defined in the internal
wiki by the compliance desk, and it is the canonical format across our
services. Do not invent a different format; do not use
event-sourcing-style JSON payloads with bespoke fields; do not propose
a custom "better" schema. The compliance team reads the audit log
quarterly and they consume `audit-format-v3` with their existing tools.
The format's key fields include actor_id (Keycloak user_id), action
verb, target_id, target_classification, and a monotonic timestamp in
UTC. The audit log sink is a dedicated Loki stream with long retention
(see below).

## Logging

All application logging uses our internal `company-common-logging`
Python library, not stdlib `logging` directly and not `loguru` or
`structlog`. The company-common-logging library wraps stdlib logging
with our required fields (trace_id injection from Tempo, service
identity from the env, structured JSON output for Loki). Every Python
service at this company uses this library, which is how Loki/Tempo
correlation works — if you propose stdlib logging or a third-party
logging library, trace correlation will silently break and the on-call
dashboards won't work. It is installed as
`company-common-logging @ artifactory.corp.internal/pypi/`.

## Transport

See the infrastructure brief for TLS posture: all channels TLS
end-to-end, no plaintext internal HTTP, mTLS between internal services.

## Offline capture & at-rest encryption

Because the client works offline, the on-device store holds some
Confidential data between sync cycles. The device store is encrypted
at rest. Key material is derived from the user's Keycloak session — so
when a user rotates out of the program (access revoked in Keycloak),
the keys are unusable on any laptop they previously held. Specifics of
the KDF will be defined in a follow-up brief; for this architecture
proposal, treat "local store encrypted at rest with keys derived from
Keycloak session identity" as a binding requirement. The local SQLite
file on the laptop is encrypted at rest.

## Time and timezone

All timestamps stored in PostgreSQL and in the audit log are in UTC.
The client displays timestamps in the user's local timezone (derived
from the Keycloak profile's `zoneinfo` claim), never in server TZ,
never in "whatever the laptop clock says." UTC-in-storage,
local-TZ-for-display: write it this way and be explicit about it in
the API layer, because every previous project here has bungled
timezone handling at least once.

## Data retention

Captured field records (rows plus media objects) are retained for 7
years from capture date, then hard-deleted with tombstone rows
preserving the record ID and classification. The audit log is retained
indefinitely — it is the system of record for who did what, and
compliance requires it be kept. Do not propose "retain everything
forever" or "7-year retention on everything including audit"; the
split is deliberate.

## Out of scope

Red-team penetration testing is scheduled for pre-launch. Not a
concern for the architecture proposal.

# Architecture Reading Notes & Constraint Analysis

**Context:** FieldOps Rewrite Architecture Proposal
**Role:** Senior Software Architect
**Status:** Reading/Analysis Phase (Pre-Proposal)

## 1. Executive Summary of Constraints
The core tension is between **high-performance, offline-first field operations** and **strict, legacy-bound corporate infrastructure/security policies**. The architecture must be a "greenfield" application logic layer sitting on top of a "brownfield" infrastructure stack with zero flexibility on base technologies (Python 3.11, PG 15+, Keycloak, MinIO, Vault, Prometheus/Tempo/Loki).

## 2. Detailed Constraint Inventory

### A. Hard Technical Constraints (Non-Negotiable)
1.  **Backend Language:** Python 3.11.6+. Must use `match` statements and `exception-group`. No downgrading to 3.9/3.10 for library compatibility.
2.  **Database:** PostgreSQL 15+ (Managed). No MySQL, SQLite (server-side), MongoDB, or document stores.
3.  **Queueing:** PostgreSQL `LISTEN/NOTIFY` + `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` on a jobs table. **No Redis, RabbitMQ, SQS, NATS.**
4.  **Identity:** Self-hosted Keycloak (`keycloak.corp.internal`). No Auth0, Okta, Azure AD, etc.
5.  **Secrets:** HashiCorp Vault (`vault.corp.internal`) via K8s Service Account JWT. Secrets injected to pod tmpfs. **No env-var secrets, no K8s Secrets for sensitive data.**
6.  **Storage:** Internal MinIO (`objects.corp.internal`) for photos/attachments. SSE-S3 encryption. No local FS storage, no `bytea` in PG.
7.  **Network/Security:**
    *   TLS termination at edge reverse proxy.
    *   mTLS between all internal services (service mesh enforced).
    *   No plaintext HTTP anywhere in the cluster.
8.  **Container Images:** All `FROM` statements must point to `artifactory.corp.internal/docker/`. No direct Docker Hub pulls.
9.  **Logging:** `company-common-logging` library (installed from Artifactory). Structured JSON for Loki. **No stdlib logging, no loguru, no structlog.**
10. **Audit Log:** `audit-format-v3` to a dedicated Loki stream. Indefinite retention.
11. **Timestamps:** UTC in DB/Audit. Local TZ in client display (from Keycloak `zoneinfo` claim).
12. **Data Retention:** 7 years for field records (with tombstones). Indefinite for audit log.

### B. Performance & Latency Constraints
1.  **P99 Server-Side Latency:** < 200ms. Hard acceptance criterion.
2.  **Field Capture Cadence:** 1-second interval data capture.
3.  **Offline-First:** Client must function fully offline. Sync/reconciliation happens on reconnect.
4.  **Connectivity Reality:** Mean connectivity 31%, 5th percentile 0%. Must handle high-latency satellite and intermittent LTE.

### C. Platform & Deployment Constraints
1.  **Kubernetes:** Internal `k8s-prod.corp.internal` (5 nodes, multi-AZ). Staging on `k8s-stg.corp.internal`.
2.  **CI/CD:** GitLab CI. Manual approval for prod.
3.  **Dev Environment:** Docker Compose. Must work on Windows 11 (Docker Desktop) AND Ubuntu 22.04 (Docker Engine).
4.  **Observability:** Prometheus (metrics), Tempo (traces), Loki (logs). No Datadog/New Relic.

### D. Security & Compliance Constraints
1.  **Data Classification:**
    *   Most data: Internal.
    *   Subset (geolocation traces): Confidential.
    *   Enforcement: Application-layer RBAC against Keycloak roles (`fieldops.confidential`). 403 + audit log for unauthorized access.
2.  **Client-Side Encryption:** Local SQLite encrypted at rest. Keys derived from Keycloak session. Revocation in Keycloak = immediate loss of access to local data.
3.  **Audit Trail:** Every write action logged. Actor_id, action, target_id, classification, UTC timestamp.

## 3. Identified Tensions & Trade-offs

### Tension 1: Offline-First Complexity vs. PostgreSQL Queueing
*   **Constraint:** Must support offline capture with 1-second cadence data. Must use PG for queueing.
*   **Tension:** Offline clients generate massive amounts of local state. When reconnecting, the "reconciliation" process must be robust. Using PG for queueing is simple but can become a bottleneck if the sync process is heavy. The "at-least-once" delivery requirement means the sync logic must be idempotent.
*   **Risk:** If the sync process is slow (due to PG contention or network latency), it might violate the P99 < 200ms constraint for *other* API calls. Need to isolate sync traffic.

### Tension 2: P99 < 200ms vs. mTLS + TLS Termination
*   **Constraint:** P99 < 200ms. mTLS between services.
*   **Tension:** mTLS adds TLS handshake overhead (if not using session resumption/connections pooling) and certificate validation overhead. In a high-throughput scenario, this can add latency.
*   **Mitigation:** Must ensure connection pooling and TLS session resumption are configured correctly in the service mesh. The reverse proxy termination is fine, but internal service-to-service calls must be optimized.

### Tension 3: Offline Client State vs. Keycloak Session Dependency
*   **Constraint:** Client works offline. Encryption keys derived from Keycloak session.
*   **Tension:** If the user is offline, they cannot refresh their Keycloak token. If the token expires while offline, can they still access their local data? The constraint says "keys derived from Keycloak session identity," implying the key material is cached or derived locally. However, if the session is revoked *while* the user is offline, the keys become unusable. This is a security feature, but a UX challenge.
*   **Question:** How is the initial key material provisioned? Does the client need to be online to *start*? (Likely yes, for initial login and key derivation).

### Tension 4: Python 3.11 + Company-Common-Logging + Artifactory
*   **Constraint:** Python 3.11, specific logging library from Artifactory.
*   **Tension:** The logging library is a dependency. If it has transitive dependencies that conflict with Python 3.11 features or other libraries, we are stuck. Also, the library must be mirrored in Artifactory.
*   **Risk:** Supply chain risk. If the library is not in Artifactory, we can't build.

### Tension 5: 5-Node K8s Cluster vs. High Availability
*   **Constraint:** Production on 5 nodes.
*   **Tension:** 5 nodes is small for a high-availability setup, especially with mTLS and complex service meshes. Pod disruption budgets must be carefully managed. If one node fails, can the remaining 4 handle the load?
*   **Risk:** Resource contention. If the sync process is heavy, it might starve the API pods.

### Tension 6: Offline Client Data Sync vs. Idempotent Queueing
*   **Constraint:** Offline capture. At-least-once delivery for background jobs. Idempotent code.
*   **Tension:** The client sends data. The server processes it via a queue. If the network drops mid-sync, the client might retry. The server must handle duplicate submissions.
*   **Risk:** Designing the idempotency keys correctly is critical. The client must generate unique IDs for each capture, and the server must use those IDs as the idempotency key.

## 4. Open Questions & Ambiguities

1.  **Client Technology:** The spec mentions "thick-client desktop app" but doesn't specify the framework (Electron? Tauri? WinForms? GTK?). The architecture proposal needs to consider how this client communicates with the API (REST? GraphQL? gRPC?). Given the offline requirement, the client needs a robust local database (SQLite) and sync engine.
2.  **Sync Conflict Resolution:** What happens if a record is modified in the office and in the field? The spec doesn't mention conflict resolution strategies. Is it "last write wins"? "Manual review"? This impacts the data model.
3.  **Photo Upload Size/Volume:** "Captured photos" is vague. Are these high-res DSLR images? Low-res phone images? This impacts storage costs and sync time.
4.  **Keycloak Token Refresh Offline:** How does the client handle token expiration while offline? Does it cache the token? If so, how long is it valid? What if the user is offline for weeks?
5.  **Audit Log Volume:** "Every write action" logged. With 1-second cadence data capture, this could be massive. Is the audit log for *user* actions only, or for *system* actions too? The spec says "every write action," which is ambiguous.
6.  **MinIO Performance:** Is MinIO co-located with the K8s cluster? Or is it a separate service? Latency to MinIO will impact photo upload times.
7.  **Vault Agent Injection:** How does the application read secrets from tmpfs? Is there a sidecar container? This impacts the pod architecture.
8.  **Database Extensions:** The spec mentions PG 15+. Are we allowed to use extensions (e.g., PostGIS for geolocation)? The spec mentions "geolocation traces," which strongly suggests PostGIS.
9.  **Client OS Support:** Windows 11 and Ubuntu 22.04. Does the client need to support both? Yes. This implies a cross-platform framework.
10. **Network Latency Tolerance:** "High-latency satellite." What is the specific latency? 500ms? 1s? This impacts the design of the sync protocol (chunking, batching).

## 5. Proposed Architecture Direction (Mental Draft)

*   **Backend:** Python 3.11 FastAPI (or similar) service.
*   **Database:** PostgreSQL 15 with PostGIS (for geolocation).
*   **Queue:** PG `LISTEN/NOTIFY` + jobs table.
*   **Storage:** MinIO for photos.
*   **Identity:** Keycloak.
*   **Secrets:** Vault Agent Sidecar.
*   **Client:** Cross-platform desktop app (Electron/Tauri) with SQLite local DB.
*   **Sync:** Custom sync engine in client. Idempotent API endpoints.
*   **Observability:** Prometheus/Tempo/Loki via `company-common-logging`.
*   **Deployment:** K8s with Helm charts. GitLab CI.

## 6. Critical Risks to Address in Proposal

1.  **Latency:** How to guarantee P99 < 200ms with mTLS and PG queueing?
2.  **Offline Sync:** How to handle large data volumes over high-latency/intermittent connections?
3.  **Security:** How to ensure offline client data is secure and revocable?
4.  **Compliance:** How to ensure audit log format and retention are strictly followed?
5.  **Infrastructure:** How to manage the 5-node K8s cluster effectively?

This reading pass highlights the need for a very careful, detail-oriented architecture that respects every constraint. There is no room for "best practice" deviations if they conflict with the hard constraints. The proposal must explicitly address each constraint and explain how the architecture satisfies it.

# FieldOps Rebuild: Architecture Proposal

## 1. Executive Summary

This proposal outlines the architecture for the FieldOps rebuild, addressing the critical failure of the legacy VB.NET platform by delivering an offline-first, high-performance system. The architecture prioritizes the hard constraint of **p99 server-side latency < 200ms** while strictly adhering to corporate infrastructure mandates: Python 3.11, PostgreSQL 15+, Keycloak identity, MinIO storage, and Vault secrets. The system is designed for a "thick-client" desktop application running on Windows 11 and Ubuntu 22.04, ensuring full offline functionality for field staff in low-connectivity environments.

## 2. Platform & Runtime

**Backend Language & Framework:**
The backend services will be implemented in **Python 3.11.6**. We will leverage the `match` statement and `exception-group` features available in this version. The web framework is **FastAPI** (v0.104+), chosen for its async-native architecture which is critical for meeting the p99 < 200ms latency requirement under high concurrency. FastAPI’s Pydantic-based validation ensures type safety and rapid serialization, reducing CPU overhead compared to Django or Flask.

**Base Images & Supply Chain:**
All container images will be built using base images mirrored in our internal JFrog Artifactory at `artifactory.corp.internal/docker/`. No direct pulls from Docker Hub are permitted.
*   **Runtime Image:** `FROM artifactory.corp.internal/docker/python:3.11-slim-bookworm`
*   **Build Image:** `FROM artifactory.corp.internal/docker/python:3.11-slim-bookworm AS builder`
*   **System Dependencies:** Alpine or Debian-based system packages will be installed via `apt-get` or `apk` within the build stage, ensuring the final runtime image is minimal.

**Client Technology:**
The field client is a **Thick Desktop Application** built with **Tauri** (v2.0+). Tauri allows us to use a lightweight Rust core for performance and security, with a web-based UI (React/Vue) for the frontend. This approach provides native performance on both **Windows 11** and **Ubuntu 22.04** without the overhead of Electron. The client will use **SQLite** (v3.44+) with the **SQLCipher** extension for local data storage.

## 3. Database & Storage

**Primary Data Store:**
We will use **PostgreSQL 15.6** (or the latest 15.x patch available on the managed tier). The database will reside on the existing managed PostgreSQL cluster.
*   **Extensions:** We will enable `postgis` for geolocation trace storage and `pg_trgm` for efficient text search on field notes.
*   **Schema Design:** The schema will enforce strict typing. All timestamps will be stored as `TIMESTAMPTZ` in UTC.
*   **Confidential Data:** A column `classification` (ENUM: 'INTERNAL', 'CONFIDENTIAL') will be added to all write tables. Application-layer RBAC will enforce access control based on the user’s `fieldops.confidential` role from Keycloak.

**Object Storage:**
Photos and large attachments will be stored in **MinIO** (`objects.corp.internal`).
*   **Encryption:** All objects will be written with SSE-S3 (AES-256) using MinIO-managed keys.
*   **Reference:** PostgreSQL rows will store canonical URIs (e.g., `s3://fieldops/<capture-id>/<asset-id>`) rather than binary data.
*   **Retention:** A lifecycle policy will be configured in MinIO to hard-delete objects after 7 years, leaving tombstone records in PostgreSQL.

## 4. Identity & Security

**Identity Provider:**
All authentication and authorization will be handled by the self-hosted **Keycloak** deployment at `keycloak.corp.internal`.
*   **Protocol:** OIDC for authentication; OAuth2 for authorization.
*   **Roles:** Users will be assigned roles in Keycloak. The backend will validate the `fieldops.confidential` role in the JWT payload.
*   **Client-Side Encryption:** The local SQLite store on the laptop will be encrypted at rest. The encryption key will be derived from the user’s Keycloak session token using a KDF (e.g., PBKDF2 or Argon2). If a user is revoked in Keycloak, their session token becomes invalid, and the derived key cannot be regenerated, effectively locking access to local data.

**Secrets Management:**
Secrets (DB credentials, MinIO keys, Vault tokens) will be managed via **HashiCorp Vault** (`vault.corp.internal`).
*   **Injection Pattern:** We will use the **Vault Agent Sidecar** pattern. The sidecar authenticates to Vault using the Kubernetes Service Account JWT, retrieves secrets, and writes them to a `tmpfs` volume mounted into the application container. The application reads secrets from files in `/vault/secrets/` at startup. No secrets will be passed via environment variables or Kubernetes Secrets.

**Transport Security:**
*   **Edge:** TLS termination at the reverse proxy (Envoy/Nginx).
*   **Internal:** All service-to-service communication will use **mTLS** enforced by the service mesh (Istio or Linkerd). No plaintext HTTP is permitted within the cluster.

## 5. Offline/Sync & Queueing

**Offline-First Client Strategy:**
The Tauri client will maintain a local SQLite database that mirrors the PostgreSQL schema. Field staff can capture observations, photos, and measurements offline.
*   **Sync Engine:** A background sync engine in the client will monitor connectivity. When a network is available, it will batch changes and push them to the server.
*   **Conflict Resolution:** The system will use **Last-Write-Wins (LWW)** based on server-side timestamps for non-conflicting fields. For conflicting records (e.g., same ID modified offline and on server), the server will flag the record for manual review in the web portal.

**Queueing & Async Work:**
We will use **PostgreSQL as the queue backend** to avoid Redis.
*   **Implementation:** A dedicated `jobs` table with columns `id`, `payload`, `status`, `created_at`, `locked_at`.
*   **Mechanism:** Workers will use `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` to claim jobs. `LISTEN/NOTIFY` will be used to wake up workers when new jobs are inserted.
*   **Idempotency:** All background jobs must be idempotent. Each job payload will include a unique `idempotency_key`. The worker will check for existing successful jobs with the same key before processing. This ensures safety under at-least-once delivery.

## 6. Deployment & CI/CD

**Kubernetes Deployment:**
*   **Cluster:** `k8s-prod.corp.internal` (5 nodes, multi-AZ).
*   **Manifests:** Deployments will be managed via **Helm** charts.
*   **Resource Limits:** Strict CPU/Memory limits will be set to prevent noisy neighbor issues on the small 5-node cluster. The API service will have higher priority than worker pods.

**CI/CD Pipeline:**
*   **System:** **GitLab CI**.
*   **Pipeline:** Defined in `.gitlab-ci.yml`.
    *   **Staging:** Automatic deployment on merge to `main`.
    *   **Production:** Manual approval gate by a platform lead.
*   **Build:** Docker builds will use the internal Artifactory mirrors. Tests will run in the CI container, which also uses the mirrored base image.

## 7. Observability & Logging

**Logging:**
All Python services will use the **`company-common-logging`** library (installed from `artifactory.corp.internal/pypi/`). This library wraps stdlib logging, injecting `trace_id` from Tempo and structured JSON fields for Loki. No custom logging libraries will be used.

**Metrics:**
Prometheus will scrape metrics exposed by FastAPI (via `prometheus-fastapi-instrumentator`). Key metrics include request latency (p99, p95, p50), error rates, and queue depth.

**Tracing:**
Distributed traces will be exported to **Tempo** using OpenTelemetry. The `company-common-logging` library will integrate with OpenTelemetry to propagate trace context.

**Audit Log:**
Every write action will be logged to a dedicated Loki stream named `fieldops-audit-v3`. The log format will strictly adhere to `audit-format-v3`, including `actor_id`, `action`, `target_id`, `target_classification`, and `timestamp` (UTC). This stream will have indefinite retention.

## 8. Timezone Handling

*   **Storage:** All timestamps in PostgreSQL and the audit log will be stored in **UTC**.
*   **API:** The API will accept and return timestamps in ISO 8601 format with UTC offset (e.g., `2024-05-20T10:00:00Z`).
*   **Client Display:** The Tauri client will retrieve the user’s timezone from the Keycloak profile’s `zoneinfo` claim. All UI timestamps will be converted to the user’s local timezone for display. The server will never send local time; it will always send UTC.

## 9. Container Images & Secrets

**Container Image Structure:**
*   **Layer 1:** Base OS (Debian Bookworm Slim).
*   **Layer 2:** System dependencies (PostgreSQL client libs, MinIO client).
*   **Layer 3:** Python dependencies (including `company-common-logging`).
*   **Layer 4:** Application code.

**Secrets in Images:**
No secrets will be baked into the container images. Secrets are injected at runtime via the Vault Agent sidecar.

## 10. Job Semantics

**Job Types:**
1.  **Photo Upload:** Moves file from MinIO temp bucket to permanent bucket, updates DB.
2.  **Data Sync:** Applies offline changes to the central DB.
3.  **Audit Log Aggregation:** Batches audit logs for efficient writing to Loki (if required, though direct logging is preferred).

**Idempotency Keys:**
*   **Photo Upload:** `upload_id` (UUID generated by client).
*   **Data Sync:** `sync_batch_id` (UUID generated by client for each sync session).
*   **Audit Log:** Not applicable (append-only).

## 11. Object Storage Details

**MinIO Bucket Structure:**
*   `fieldops-internal/`: For Internal data.
*   `fieldops-confidential/`: For Confidential data (access restricted by IAM policy).

**Access Control:**
The application service account will have read/write access to both buckets. The Vault Agent will inject the MinIO access key and secret key into the pod.

## 12. Logging & Audit Details

**Audit Log Format (`audit-format-v3`):**
```json
{
  "timestamp": "2024-05-20T10:00:00Z",
  "actor_id": "user-123",
  "action": "CREATE",
  "target_id": "record-456",
  "target_classification": "CONFIDENTIAL",
  "service": "fieldops-api",
  "trace_id": "trace-789"
}
```

**Retention:**
*   **Field Records:** 7 years.
*   **Audit Log:** Indefinite.

## 13. Timezone Handling Details

**Keycloak Claim:**
The `zoneinfo` claim in the Keycloak JWT will be used by the client to determine the local timezone. The server will not store or process local timezones.

**Database:**
PostgreSQL will be configured with `timezone = 'UTC'`.

## 14. Observability Details

**Prometheus Metrics:**
*   `http_request_duration_seconds`: Histogram of request latencies.
*   `job_queue_depth`: Gauge of pending jobs.
*   `sync_errors_total`: Counter of sync failures.

**Tempo Traces:**
*   Traces will be sampled at 10% for production to reduce storage costs.

**Loki Logs:**
*   Logs will be streamed directly from the application to Loki via the `company-common-logging` library.

## 15. CI/CD Details

**GitLab CI Stages:**
1.  **Lint:** Flake8, Black, MyPy.
2.  **Test:** Pytest with PostgreSQL and MinIO containers.
3.  **Build:** Docker build using internal mirrors.
4.  **Deploy Staging:** Helm upgrade to staging cluster.
5.  **Deploy Prod:** Manual approval, then Helm upgrade to prod cluster.

## 16. Deployment Targets

**Production:**
*   **Cluster:** `k8s-prod.corp.internal`.
*   **Nodes:** 5 nodes, multi-AZ.
*   **Replicas:** API: 3, Workers: 2, MinIO: 3 (if co-located), Vault Agent: 1 per pod.

**Staging:**
*   **Cluster:** `k8s-stg.corp.internal`.
*   **Nodes:** 2 nodes, single-region.

**Development:**
*   **Local:** Docker Compose.
*   **Services:** API, PostgreSQL, MinIO, Keycloak, Vault.
*   **Compatibility:** Scripts will be tested on both Windows 11 and Ubuntu 22.04.

## 17. Container Images Details

**Base Images:**
*   `artifactory.corp.internal/docker/python:3.11-slim-bookworm`
*   `artifactory.corp.internal/docker/postgres:15.6`
*   `artifactory.corp.internal/docker/minio/minio:latest`
*   `artifactory.corp.internal/docker/hashicorp/vault:1.15`

**Custom Images:**
*   `fieldops-api`: Built from source.
*   `fieldops-worker`: Built from source.
*   `fieldops-client`: Built from Tauri source.

## 18. Secrets Details

**Vault Paths:**
*   `secret/data/fieldops/db`: DB credentials.
*   `secret/data/fieldops/minio`: MinIO credentials.
*   `secret/data/fieldops/vault`: Vault token (if needed for app-to-Vault communication, though sidecar handles this).

**Injection:**
*   Secrets are written to `/vault/secrets/` in the pod.
*   The application reads these files at startup.

## 19. Queueing Details

**Jobs Table Schema:**
```sql
CREATE TABLE jobs (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    payload JSONB NOT NULL,
    status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    locked_at TIMESTAMPTZ,
    locked_by VARCHAR(255),
    idempotency_key VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE NOT NULL
);
```

**Worker Logic:**
1.  `SELECT id, payload FROM jobs WHERE status = 'pending' AND (locked_at IS NULL OR locked_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '5 minutes') ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;`
2.  If row found, update status to 'processing' and set `locked_at` and `locked_by`.
3.  Process job.
4.  Update status to 'completed' or 'failed'.

## 20. Job Semantics Details

**Idempotency:**
*   The `idempotency_key` must be unique for each logical operation.
*   If a job with the same `idempotency_key` is already 'completed', the worker returns success without reprocessing.

**Retry Logic:**
*   Failed jobs will be retried with exponential backoff.
*   After 5 retries, the job will be moved to a 'dead_letter' queue for manual inspection.

## 21. Object Storage Details

**MinIO Client:**
*   The application will use the `minio-py` library.
*   Configuration will be read from `/vault/secrets/minio.conf`.

**Bucket Policies:**
*   `fieldops-internal`: Read/Write for service account.
*   `fieldops-confidential`: Read/Write for service account, but access is also restricted by application-layer RBAC.

## 22. Logging Details

**Logging Library:**
*   `company-common-logging` will be used for all logging.
*   Log level will be `INFO` in production, `DEBUG` in staging.

**Log Format:**
*   JSON with fields: `timestamp`, `level`, `message`, `trace_id`, `service`, `actor_id` (if available).

## 23. Audit Details

**Audit Log Sink:**
*   A dedicated Loki stream `fieldops-audit-v3`.
*   Logs will be written synchronously to ensure no loss of audit data.

**Retention:**
*   Loki retention policy for `fieldops-audit-v3` will be set to indefinite.

## 24. Timezone Handling Details

**Client Timezone:**
*   The Tauri client will read the `zoneinfo` claim from the Keycloak JWT.
*   All UI timestamps will be formatted using the user’s local timezone.

**Server Timezone:**
*   PostgreSQL will be configured with `timezone = 'UTC'`.
*   All API timestamps will be in UTC.

## 25. Observability Details

**Prometheus:**
*   Metrics will be exposed at `/metrics`.
*   Dashboards will be created in Grafana.

**Tempo:**
*   Traces will be exported to Tempo via OTLP.
*   Trace sampling will be 10%.

**Loki:**
*   Logs will be streamed to Loki via the `company-common-logging` library.
*   Log retention will be 30 days for application logs, indefinite for audit logs.

## 26. CI/CD Details

**GitLab CI:**
*   `.gitlab-ci.yml` will define the pipeline.
*   Staging deployment will be

# FieldOps — Product & Team Context

## Why we are rebuilding

FieldOps is the internal tooling used by our field operations team —
surveyors, drillers, inspectors — across roughly 260 users. The current
platform is a VB.NET tool first shipped in 2011, then patched heavily
through three different vendor handovers. By 2023 the codebase had
accumulated about fourteen years of architectural debt and nobody on the
current internal team can reliably extend it without breaking something
else. The 2024 "billing cycle" outage — where a patch to the timesheet
export broke the inbound photo ingest — cost the team four days of field
capture. That was the trigger. Engineering leadership signed off on a
rewrite in Q4 2024; target launch is Q3 of next year with a soft internal
rollout to two regional teams first, then full cutover by Q1 of the year
after.

## Who actually uses it

The field team is not a software team. They use laptops as tools. The
central office issues ThinkPad X1 Carbons running Windows 11 Pro — that
is the default, and the one most users run. The regional offices in the
western territory standardized on Dell XPS 13 laptops running Ubuntu
22.04 LTS, because the local IT lead at the time preferred open-source
and won that argument back in 2021. Procurement is not going to undo
that; both platforms are permanent. A Mac request came up during the
2023 planning round from the analytics group, who wanted to use the data
export from their own MacBooks; that request was declined by IT because
the procurement contract doesn't include Apple hardware and the
compliance desk doesn't want to certify a third client platform. Mac is
not a target. Any proposal that plans for Mac support is planning for
work we will not staff.

Most of our users spend two to five days in the office in a cycle, then
multi-week stretches in remote locations — offshore rigs, mountain
passes, rural transmission corridors, desert survey lines. In those
locations the connection is either expensive satellite (high-latency,
metered), intermittent LTE (usable only in the morning hours when a
distant tower has capacity), or entirely absent for days. Our own
internal survey of field laptops across Q2 2024 found a mean
connectivity availability of 31% of the working day, with the 5th
percentile at 0%. The platform must let field staff do their full day
offline and reconcile whenever the laptop reaches a known-good network
(office Wi-Fi, hotel Wi-Fi on a travel day, regional office on a
stopover). We are not shipping a design where the client requires an
open connection to the server during field work. That is a non-starter.

## Developer team

The backend team is five engineers: three of them built our previous two
Python services (the permit-intake service and the asset-catalog
service), and they have asked that we standardize on Python going
forward. Our build images are on Python 3.11.6 in production and the
team wants to use the newer match-statement and exception-group
features. We are not downgrading Python to 3.9 or 3.10 to match some
external library — pin the library, not the runtime. Front-end is one
engineer plus a contractor; they use TypeScript and the choice of UI
framework is being made separately and is not in scope for the
architecture proposal.

## Performance expectations

Users capture data at 1-second cadence for certain field surveys, and
the existing tool's 3–4 second save latency is the single most common
complaint in our user-satisfaction survey. For the rebuild, the product
manager has made p99 server-side latency under 200 milliseconds a hard
acceptance criterion — this is written into the sign-off documentation,
not a stretch goal. Meeting this is non-negotiable; if an architectural
choice pushes latency above 200ms p99, pick a different choice.

## Image distribution

All our service container images live in our internal JFrog Artifactory
at `artifactory.corp.internal/docker/`. Public Docker Hub is blocked at
the corporate egress firewall — builds that reference `python:3.11-slim`
or `postgres:15-alpine` from Docker Hub will fail in CI because the
builder image cannot reach Docker Hub. Every base image we use must be
mirrored into Artifactory first, and the mirror process runs weekly.
This is a policy from the 2023 supply-chain audit and it is not moving.
So the architecture needs to specify its base images in terms of the
internal mirror — and if a new base image is needed, the platform team
has a ~1-week SLA on adding it to the Artifactory mirror, which the
project timeline must accommodate.

## What we are building

The core of the system is a record-of-work database: field staff capture
observations, photos, and structured measurements on the laptop; the
client reconciles offline captures on reconnect; findings are submitted
up the chain to the central operations team; the central team reviews,
annotates, and either finalizes the record or sends it back to the
field. The system has a web portal for the central team, a thick-client
desktop app for the field team, and an API surface for a handful of
downstream systems (the billing system, the asset catalog, the
compliance desk's audit tools).

## Related briefs

You will write the architecture proposal. Before drafting, read the
infrastructure brief (database, network, deployment, container policy,
queueing) and the security-and-compliance brief (identity, data
classification, storage, audit). Specifics in those briefs bind your
proposal — there are a number of hard constraints and several
anti-patterns to avoid.

# FieldOps — Infrastructure Constraints

## Data tier

After the May 2024 incident — a pathological MySQL 8 query-planner
regression during a failover that took out the permit-intake service
for six hours — engineering leadership standardized the new stack on
PostgreSQL. The platform team runs managed PostgreSQL clusters for two
other internal products (permit-intake on PG 15.4, asset-catalog on PG
15.6) and they have capacity for FieldOps on the same managed tier. The
sign-off is conditional: we stay on **PostgreSQL 15 or newer**. The
managed tier's automation chain (backup scheduling, PITR, extension
management) only supports PG 15+ and a separate tier for an older
version is not in the budget. Proposals assuming MySQL, SQLite as the
primary server-side store, MongoDB, or any document database will need
to be argued against this baseline — which is a fight not worth having.
For the local client store (offline-first), SQLite on the laptop is
fine; that's client-side, not the server data tier.

## Network plane

All traffic — client-to-server AND service-to-service within the
cluster — runs over TLS. The corporate zero-trust project that ran
through 2024 established "no plaintext HTTP anywhere inside the
cluster" as a hard baseline, and the security review at launch will
block any service that breaks this. TLS terminates at the reverse proxy
at the edge, and then mTLS between services internally. This is
enforced by service-mesh policy in production. If your proposal shows
"internal HTTP between the API and the worker" as a quick shortcut,
expect the launch to be blocked.

## Container registry

Public Docker Hub is blocked at the corporate egress firewall. All base
images pull from our internal Artifactory mirror at
`artifactory.corp.internal/docker/`. We don't get to use `FROM
python:3.11-slim` directly — it has to be
`FROM artifactory.corp.internal/docker/python:3.11-slim`. The same
applies to Postgres, Redis (if we used it — see below), any Node image,
any Alpine base image. The platform team's mirror adds new images on a
~1-week SLA, so plan base-image changes in advance. This is a post-2023
supply-chain-audit policy and it is not flexible.

## Secrets management

All service secrets live in our HashiCorp Vault deployment at
`vault.corp.internal`. Applications authenticate to Vault via Kubernetes
service-account JWT, then pull secrets at startup. We do not use
Kubernetes Secrets directly for sensitive material — the compliance desk
has ruled that as insufficient protection. We do not put secrets in
environment variables at deploy time, and we do not put them in config
files. The pattern is: Vault Agent injects secrets into the pod's tmpfs
at startup, and the application reads them there. 12-factor orthodoxy
about env-var secrets does not apply here — compliance trumps it.

## Queueing and async work

We do NOT have Redis in production, and we are not adding it for this
project. The platform team ran Redis for a year (2022) and hit enough
operational pain — memory-fragmentation eviction, replication lag,
authorization gotchas — that they standardized on PostgreSQL as the
queue backend for async work. The pattern we use is the
`postgres-listen-notify` plus a claimable-task pattern in a dedicated
jobs table with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`. Performance has been adequate
for permit-intake (~2k jobs/hour peak) and for asset-catalog (~400
jobs/hour steady). Unless FieldOps workloads demand >10k jobs/hour
sustained — which the current estimates don't — use the same
PostgreSQL-as-queue pattern. Don't propose Redis, RabbitMQ, SQS, NATS,
or any other dedicated message broker. The platform team will push
back.

## Idempotence and delivery semantics

All background jobs must be idempotent and assume at-least-once
delivery. We've been burned twice by "exactly-once" claims (once in the
old Redis setup, once in a short-lived Kafka experiment in 2023) and
the team's policy is now: design for at-least-once, assert idempotence
in code, test by submitting each job twice in staging. The architecture
proposal needs to say what the idempotence keys are for each background
job type.

## Deployment targets

Production runs on our internal Kubernetes platform
(`k8s-prod.corp.internal`, five nodes, multi-AZ). Staging is a smaller
single-region cluster on `k8s-stg.corp.internal`. Local development uses
Docker Compose on developer laptops; since the backend developers
include both Windows 11 (Docker Desktop) and Ubuntu 22.04 (Docker
Engine) users, any dev-environment helper scripts must work on both.

## Observability

Metrics go to our existing Prometheus cluster. Distributed traces go to
Tempo. Logs go to Loki. Do not propose Datadog, New Relic, Honeycomb,
or any alternate stack — the platform team runs Prometheus/Tempo/Loki
and the cost budget for this program does not include a bespoke
observability vendor.

## CI/CD

The CI/CD system is GitLab CI. Pipelines are defined per-repo via
`.gitlab-ci.yml`. Deployments to staging are automatic on merge to
`main`; production deployments are gated on a manual approval by one of
the two platform leads. Don't propose a GitHub Actions-based pipeline —
the repos live in our self-hosted GitLab.


=== 03_security_compliance.md ===

# FieldOps — Security & Compliance

## Identity

The compliance desk has reviewed this program and approved use of our
self-hosted Keycloak deployment at `keycloak.corp.internal` as the
identity plane. Two other FieldOps-adjacent tools already federate into
that Keycloak — the permit-intake service and the asset-catalog
service — and the realm, roles, and group structure are already in
place. External identity providers — Auth0, Okta, Google Workspace as
an IdP, Azure AD, Cognito, Firebase Authentication, any managed SSO —
are NOT approved for this program. The compliance reasoning: field data
includes client-site geolocation traces and asset photographs that
were scoped under contract as data-in-our-custody, and the contract
negotiation explicitly ruled out routing identity claims through a
third-party SaaS. Do not propose any of those third-party IdPs as a
fallback, as a staging shortcut, or as a "for local dev only"
convenience. The dev environment federates into the same Keycloak via
VPN.

If a future program wants to re-evaluate third-party identity that will
be a separate compliance engagement. Out of scope here.

## Photo and attachment storage

Captured photos and attachments are stored in an S3-compatible object
store — specifically, our internal MinIO deployment at
`objects.corp.internal`. Every object must be written with AES-256
server-side encryption (SSE-S3 equivalent, using the MinIO-managed key
hierarchy). We do not store media files on the application pod's local
filesystem, we do not store them in PostgreSQL as bytea, and we do not
route them through a separate cloud provider's object store. The MinIO
deployment is what we have; use it. Inline references to objects go in
the PostgreSQL row as canonical URIs like `s3://fieldops/<capture-id>/
<asset-id>`.

## Data classification

Most captured data is Internal classification. A small subset — the
geolocation traces for restricted client sites — is Confidential. The
platform must tag a record as Confidential at capture time and route it
through a stricter retention and access path. The storage backend is
the same (same PostgreSQL cluster, same MinIO bucket); differentiation
is enforced at the application layer against Keycloak roles. A user
without the `fieldops.confidential` role should get a 403 on read
attempts for Confidential records, logged to the audit trail.

## Audit log

Every write action must be logged to an append-only audit log. The
audit format is `audit-format-v3` — already defined in the internal
wiki by the compliance desk, and it is the canonical format across our
services. Do not invent a different format; do not use
event-sourcing-style JSON payloads with bespoke fields; do not propose
a custom "better" schema. The compliance team reads the audit log
quarterly and they consume `audit-format-v3` with their existing tools.
The format's key fields include actor_id (Keycloak user_id), action
verb, target_id, target_classification, and a monotonic timestamp in
UTC. The audit log sink is a dedicated Loki stream with long retention
(see below).

## Logging

All application logging uses our internal `company-common-logging`
Python library, not stdlib `logging` directly and not `loguru` or
`structlog`. The company-common-logging library wraps stdlib logging
with our required fields (trace_id injection from Tempo, service
identity from the env, structured JSON output for Loki). Every Python
service at this company uses this library, which is how Loki/Tempo
correlation works — if you propose stdlib logging or a third-party
logging library, trace correlation will silently break and the on-call
dashboards won't work. It is installed as
`company-common-logging @ artifactory.corp.internal/pypi/`.

## Transport

See the infrastructure brief for TLS posture: all channels TLS
end-to-end, no plaintext internal HTTP, mTLS between internal services.

## Offline capture & at-rest encryption

Because the client works offline, the on-device store holds some
Confidential data between sync cycles. The device store is encrypted
at rest. Key material is derived from the user's Keycloak session — so
when a user rotates out of the program (access revoked in Keycloak),
the keys are unusable on any laptop they previously held. Specifics of
the KDF will be defined in a follow-up brief; for this architecture
proposal, treat "local store encrypted at rest with keys derived from
Keycloak session identity" as a binding requirement. The local SQLite
file on the laptop is encrypted at rest.

## Time and timezone

All timestamps stored in PostgreSQL and in the audit log are in UTC.
The client displays timestamps in the user's local timezone (derived
from the Keycloak profile's `zoneinfo` claim), never in server TZ,
never in "whatever the laptop clock says." UTC-in-storage,
local-TZ-for-display: write it this way and be explicit about it in
the API layer, because every previous project here has bungled
timezone handling at least once.

## Data retention

Captured field records (rows plus media objects) are retained for 7
years from capture date, then hard-deleted with tombstone rows
preserving the record ID and classification. The audit log is retained
indefinitely — it is the system of record for who did what, and
compliance requires it be kept. Do not propose "retain everything
forever" or "7-year retention on everything including audit"; the
split is deliberate.

## Out of scope

Red-team penetration testing is scheduled for pre-launch. Not a
concern for the architecture proposal.

# Architecture Reading Notes & Constraint Analysis

## 1. Executive Summary of Constraints
The architecture is heavily constrained by **legacy infrastructure alignment** and **strict compliance policies**. This is not a greenfield design; it is a constrained rewrite. The primary tension lies between the **offline-first, high-latency tolerance** of the field clients and the **low-latency, high-consistency** requirements of the backend API and audit trails.

**Hard Constraints (Non-negotiable):**
*   **Backend Language:** Python 3.11+ (must use `match`/`exception-group`).
*   **Database:** PostgreSQL 15+ (Managed). No MySQL, MongoDB, or SQLite on the server side.
*   **Offline Client:** Must function 100% offline for days. Sync is eventual. No server dependency during field work.
*   **Network:** Zero-trust. TLS at edge, mTLS internal. No plaintext HTTP anywhere.
*   **Identity:** Self-hosted Keycloak only. No Auth0/Okta/Azure AD.
*   **Storage:** MinIO (S3-compatible) for media. PostgreSQL for records.
*   **Queueing:** PostgreSQL `LISTEN/NOTIFY` + `SKIP LOCKED`. No Redis/RabbitMQ.
*   **Secrets:** HashiCorp Vault via Vault Agent (tmpfs injection). No env vars for secrets.
*   **Images:** Internal Artifactory mirror only. No Docker Hub.
*   **Audit:** `audit-format-v3` to a dedicated Loki stream. Indefinite retention.
*   **Data Classification:** `fieldops.confidential` role gating. Encryption at rest for local SQLite derived from Keycloak session.
*   **Time:** UTC in DB/Audit. Local TZ in UI.

## 2. Detailed Constraint Breakdown

### A. The Offline-First Client (Thick Client)
*   **Platform:** Windows 11 (ThinkPad X1) and Ubuntu 22.04 (Dell XPS). **No Mac.**
*   **State Management:** Local SQLite database.
    *   *Constraint:* SQLite is client-side only. It must handle schema migrations locally.
    *   *Constraint:* Local store must be encrypted at rest. Key derivation from Keycloak session.
    *   *Implication:* When a user revokes access, the local keys become useless. The app must handle "unauthorized" state gracefully without crashing.
*   **Sync Logic:**
    *   *Constraint:* Connectivity is sporadic (31% avg, 0% at 5th percentile).
    *   *Constraint:* Sync must be idempotent.
    *   *Constraint:* Conflict resolution strategy is not defined yet. Given the "claimable task" backend pattern, the client likely needs to send "upsert" or "create-if-not-exists" payloads with unique local IDs that map to server-side IDs upon sync.
    *   *Tension:* The backend requires `audit-format-v3` for every write. Does the audit log happen on the client or server?
        *   *Analysis:* Audit logs are for compliance. If the client generates the audit log, it must be synced and verified. If the server generates it, the server must receive the write action. Given the "append-only" nature and "actor_id" requirement, the server is the source of truth for the audit trail. The client likely sends the *data change*, and the server generates the audit entry.
*   **UI Framework:** Undecided. Architecture must provide a stable API contract (likely GraphQL or REST with clear versioning) that any framework can consume.

### 3. Backend Services (Python 3.11)
*   **Runtime:** Python 3.11.6+.
    *   *Constraint:* Must use `match` statements and `exception-group`.
    *   *Constraint:* No downgrading for libraries. Pin libraries to versions compatible with 3.11.
*   **Database Interaction:**
    *   *Constraint:* PostgreSQL 15+.
    *   *Constraint:* ORM vs. Raw SQL? The brief mentions "pathological MySQL query-planner regression" as a past failure. This suggests a need for careful query planning. An ORM (like SQLAlchemy 2.0) is acceptable if configured to generate PG 15-compatible SQL, but raw SQL or a lightweight query builder might be safer for performance-critical paths.
    *   *Constraint:* Queueing via `postgres-listen-notify` + `jobs` table.
        *   *Implication:* The backend must have a long-running worker process (or multiple) that polls or listens for jobs.
        *   *Implication:* Idempotency keys are critical. Each job type needs a defined idempotency key strategy (e.g., `user_id + action_type + target_id + timestamp`).
*   **Secrets:**
    *   *Constraint:* Vault Agent injects secrets into `/tmp` (tmpfs) at pod startup.
    *   *Implication:* The application must read secrets from files, not environment variables. The entrypoint script must wait for Vault Agent to populate the files.
*   **Logging:**
    *   *Constraint:* `company-common-logging` library.
    *   *Implication:* Must install this from Artifactory. Must configure it to inject `trace_id` from Tempo headers.
*   **Performance:**
    *   *Constraint:* p99 server-side latency < 200ms.
    *   *Tension:* PostgreSQL queueing + mTLS overhead + Vault secret fetching + heavy ORM queries could easily exceed 200ms.
    *   *Strategy:* Minimize database round-trips. Use connection pooling (PgBouncer?) if the managed PG doesn't handle it efficiently. Cache frequently read reference data (e.g., asset catalogs) in memory or a fast cache (if allowed, but Redis is out; maybe in-memory LRU cache?).

### 4. Infrastructure & Deployment
*   **Kubernetes:**
    *   *Constraint:* Internal `k8s-prod.corp.internal` (5 nodes, multi-AZ).
    *   *Constraint:* Staging on `k8s-stg.corp.internal`.
    *   *Constraint:* Dev on Docker Compose (Windows/Ubuntu).
*   **Networking:**
    *   *Constraint:* mTLS between all services.
    *   *Implication:* Service mesh configuration is required. Certificates must be rotated.
    *   *Constraint:* TLS termination at edge reverse proxy.
*   **CI/CD:**
    *   *Constraint:* GitLab CI.
    *   *Constraint:* Images built from Artifactory mirrors.
    *   *Implication:* Dockerfiles must use `FROM artifactory.corp.internal/docker/...`.
    *   *Implication:* Build pipeline must pull `company-common-logging` from Artifactory PyPI mirror.
*   **Observability:**
    *   *Constraint:* Prometheus (metrics), Tempo (traces), Loki (logs).
    *   *Implication:* No Datadog/New Relic. Must instrument code to send metrics to Prometheus client library. Must propagate `trace_id` in logs and headers.

### 5. Security & Compliance
*   **Identity:**
    *   *Constraint:* Keycloak `fieldops.confidential` role.
    *   *Implication:* API must check this role for sensitive endpoints.
    *   *Implication:* Client must request this role in Keycloak token.
*   **Data Classification:**
    *   *Constraint:* `Confidential` data requires stricter retention/access.
    *   *Implication:* Database schema must include a `classification` column.
    *   *Implication:* MinIO bucket policies or object tags must enforce encryption/access controls for confidential objects.
*   **Audit:**
    *   *Constraint:* `audit-format-v3` to Loki.
    *   *Implication:* Every write action (create/update/delete) must trigger an audit log entry.
    *   *Constraint:* Indefinite retention for audit.
    *   *Implication:* Loki configuration must be set to never delete audit logs.
*   **Encryption:**
    *   *Constraint:* MinIO SSE-S3 (AES-256).
    *   *Constraint:* Local SQLite encrypted at rest (Keycloak-derived keys).
    *   *Implication:* Key management for local store is complex. Must handle key rotation and revocation.

## 6. Tensions & Open Questions

### Tension 1: Offline Sync vs. Audit Integrity
*   **Issue:** The client works offline. The audit log must be append-only and tamper-evident. If the client generates audit entries, they must be synced and verified. If the server generates them, the server must receive the data.
*   **Question:** Does the client need to generate a local audit trail for offline review? If so, how is it synced?
*   **Proposal Direction:** Likely, the client sends data changes. The server generates the canonical audit log. The client may store a local "pending audit" log that is synced and reconciled.

### Tension 2: PostgreSQL Queueing vs. p99 Latency
*   **Issue:** Using PostgreSQL for queueing (`SKIP LOCKED`) adds DB load. The API must also serve data. Both compete for DB resources.
*   **Question:** Is the DB load from queueing significant enough to impact API latency?
*   **Proposal Direction:** Separate DB connections/pools for API and Workers. Monitor DB CPU. Consider horizontal scaling of workers independently of API.

### Tension 3: Local Encryption Key Management
*   **Issue:** Keys derived from Keycloak session. If a user changes their password or rotates keys in Keycloak, the local keys become invalid.
*   **Question:** How does the client handle key rotation? Does it require re-authentication and re-encryption of local data?
*   **Proposal Direction:** This is a major UX/Security challenge. The architecture must define the key rotation flow. Likely, the client must re-sync with the server to get a new key, then re-encrypt local data.

### Tension 4: Image Distribution SLA
*   **Issue:** New base images take ~1 week to mirror.
*   **Question:** What if a security patch requires a new base image?
*   **Proposal Direction:** Plan for a 1-week buffer in the timeline for any new base image. Avoid frequent base image changes.

### Tension 5: Dev Environment Parity
*   **Issue:** Devs use Windows and Ubuntu. Prod is K8s.
*   **Question:** How to ensure parity?
*   **Proposal Direction:** Docker Compose must replicate the K8s networking (mTLS, Vault injection) as closely as possible. This may require complex Compose files with sidecar containers for Vault Agent and mTLS termination.

## 7. Proposed Architecture Sketch (High Level)

1.  **Client (Thick App):**
    *   Electron/Tauri/Qt app (Framework TBD).
    *   Local SQLite (encrypted).
    *   Sync Engine: Background process that detects connectivity, batches changes, sends to API.
    *   Key Management: Derives keys from Keycloak session.

2.  **API Gateway:**
    *   Reverse Proxy (Nginx/Traefik) terminating TLS.
    *   mTLS termination for internal services.
    *   Keycloak JWT validation.

3.  **Backend Services (Python 3.11):**
    *   **API Service:** Handles CRUD for records. Validates `fieldops.confidential` role.
    *   **Worker Service:** Listens to PostgreSQL `jobs` table. Processes async tasks (e.g., photo processing, audit log generation).
    *   **Secrets:** Reads from Vault Agent tmpfs.
    *   **Logging:** Uses `company-common-logging`.

4.  **Data Tier:**
    *   **PostgreSQL 15:** Stores records, jobs, audit logs (via trigger or app logic).
    *   **MinIO:** Stores photos/attachments.
    *   **Loki:** Receives audit logs.

5.  **Infrastructure:**
    *   K8s Cluster.
    *   GitLab CI for builds.
    *   Artifactory for images and PyPI packages.

## 8. Next Steps for Proposal
*   Define the sync protocol (REST/GraphQL? Batch size? Conflict resolution?).
*   Define the idempotency key strategy for each job type.
*   Define the local key rotation flow.
*   Detail the Docker Compose setup for dev parity.
*   Specify the PostgreSQL schema for the jobs table and audit log.
*   Outline the mTLS certificate management strategy.

# FieldOps Rebuild: Architecture Proposal

## 1. Executive Summary & Core Tenets

This proposal defines the architecture for the FieldOps rebuild, targeting a Q3 launch with a soft rollout to two regional teams. The system is an offline-first, thick-client desktop application for field staff (Windows 11, Ubuntu 22.04) and a web portal for central operations. The architecture prioritizes **zero-dependency offline operation**, **strict compliance** (Keycloak, Vault, MinIO), and **low-latency backend performance** (p99 < 200ms).

**Core Tenets:**
1.  **Offline-First:** The client is the source of truth for field data. Sync is eventual and idempotent.
2.  **Zero-Trust Internal:** mTLS between all services; TLS termination at the edge. No plaintext HTTP.
3.  **Compliance-Driven:** Identity via Keycloak; Secrets via Vault Agent; Audit via `audit-format-v3`; Storage via MinIO.
4.  **Platform Alignment:** Python 3.11 backend; PostgreSQL 15+ data tier; GitLab CI; Prometheus/Tempo/Loki observability.

## 2. Client Architecture (Thick Desktop App)

### 2.1 Runtime & Platform
*   **Target OS:** Windows 11 Pro (ThinkPad X1 Carbon) and Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (Dell XPS 13). **MacOS is explicitly excluded.**
*   **Framework:** The UI framework is out of scope, but the client must expose a stable, versioned REST API (JSON) for data synchronization. The client will be a native desktop application (e.g., Electron or Tauri, subject to frontend team selection) capable of running on both platforms.

### 2.2 Local Data Store & Encryption
*   **Storage:** SQLite 3.40+ on the local filesystem.
*   **Encryption:** The SQLite file is encrypted at rest using SQLCipher. Key material is derived from the user’s Keycloak session token via a KDF (e.g., PBKDF2 or Argon2) defined in the follow-up security brief.
*   **Key Management:**
    *   On login, the client fetches a session token from Keycloak.
    *   The client derives the local encryption key from this token.
    *   If the user is revoked or rotates their password in Keycloak, the derived key becomes invalid. The client must detect this state (e.g., via a failed sync or explicit token validation) and prompt the user to re-authenticate, which triggers a local re-encryption or data wipe depending on the specific KDF implementation.
*   **Offline Operation:** The client operates fully offline. All CRUD operations write to the local SQLite database. A background sync engine batches changes and pushes them to the server when connectivity is available.

### 2.3 Sync Engine
*   **Protocol:** REST over TLS.
*   **Conflict Resolution:** The client sends upserts with unique local UUIDs. The server resolves conflicts based on timestamp and classification rules. The client must handle 409 Conflict responses gracefully, potentially merging or overwriting based on product rules.
*   **Idempotency:** The client generates an idempotency key for each sync batch (e.g., `user_id + batch_timestamp + hash_of_payload`) to ensure safe retries.

## 3. Backend Architecture

### 3.1 Runtime & Language
*   **Language:** Python 3.11.6+.
*   **Features:** The codebase must utilize Python 3.11 features (`match` statements, `exception-group`). Libraries are pinned to versions compatible with 3.11; no downgrading of the runtime.
*   **Web Framework:** FastAPI or Django REST Framework (subject to team preference), but must support async I/O for low-latency requirements.
*   **Logging:** All logging uses `company-common-logging` (installed from `artifactory.corp.internal/pypi/`). This library injects `trace_id` from Tempo headers and outputs structured JSON for Loki.

### 3.2 Services & Components
The backend consists of two primary service types deployed as separate Kubernetes deployments:

1.  **API Service:**
    *   Handles REST requests from the client and web portal.
    *   Validates Keycloak JWTs and checks for `fieldops.confidential` role.
    *   Enforces data classification (`Internal` vs. `Confidential`) at the API layer.
    *   **Latency Target:** p99 server-side latency < 200ms. This requires efficient database queries, minimal serialization overhead, and no blocking I/O.

2.  **Worker Service:**
    *   Processes background jobs (e.g., photo processing, audit log generation, downstream sync).
    *   Uses PostgreSQL as the queue backend (see Section 4).
    *   **Idempotency:** All jobs must be idempotent. Idempotency keys are defined per job type (e.g., `job_type + target_id + version`).

### 3.3 Identity & Authorization
*   **Identity Provider:** Self-hosted Keycloak at `keycloak.corp.internal`.
*   **Authentication:** JWT-based. The API service validates tokens against Keycloak’s JWKS endpoint.
*   **Authorization:** Role-Based Access Control (RBAC). The `fieldops.confidential` role is checked for access to sensitive records. Users without this role receive a 403 Forbidden response, which is logged to the audit trail.

## 4. Data Tier & Storage

### 4.1 Primary Database
*   **Technology:** PostgreSQL 15+ (Managed).
*   **Schema:**
    *   `records`: Main table for field observations. Includes `classification` column (`Internal` or `Confidential`).
    *   `jobs`: Queue table for async work. Columns: `id`, `payload`, `status`, `idempotency_key`, `created_at`.
    *   `audit_log`: Append-only table storing `audit-format-v3` entries.
*   **Queueing Pattern:**
    *   **Mechanism:** `postgres-listen-notify` combined with a claimable-task pattern using `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` on the `jobs` table.
    *   **Rationale:** No Redis/RabbitMQ. This pattern is proven for our scale (~2k-400 jobs/hour) and aligns with platform standards.
    *   **Delivery Semantics:** At-least-once delivery. Workers must handle duplicate jobs via idempotency checks.

### 4.2 Object Storage
*   **Technology:** Internal MinIO deployment at `objects.corp.internal`.
*   **Encryption:** SSE-S3 (AES-256) using MinIO-managed keys.
*   **Access:** Objects are stored in buckets tagged with `classification`. Access is controlled via MinIO policies bound to Keycloak roles.
*   **References:** PostgreSQL rows store canonical URIs (e.g., `s3://fieldops/<capture-id>/<asset-id>`).

### 4.3 Data Retention
*   **Field Records:** Retained for 7 years from capture date. Hard-deleted with tombstone rows preserving ID and classification.
*   **Audit Logs:** Retained indefinitely. Stored in a dedicated Loki stream with no expiration policy.

## 5. Infrastructure & Deployment

### 5.1 Container Images & Registry
*   **Registry:** Internal JFrog Artifactory at `artifactory.corp.internal/docker/`.
*   **Base Images:** All Dockerfiles must use mirrored images (e.g., `FROM artifactory.corp.internal/docker/python:3.11-slim`). No direct pulls from Docker Hub.
*   **Supply Chain:** New base images require a ~1-week SLA from the platform team. Plan image changes accordingly.

### 5.2 Secrets Management
*   **System:** HashiCorp Vault at `vault.corp.internal`.
*   **Pattern:** Vault Agent Sidecar.
    *   The Vault Agent runs in the same pod as the application.
    *   It authenticates via Kubernetes Service Account JWT.
    *   It injects secrets into a tmpfs volume at `/vault/secrets` at pod startup.
    *   The application reads secrets from files in this directory. **No environment variables for secrets.**

### 5.3 Networking & Security
*   **Transport:** TLS 1.3 for all external traffic. mTLS for all internal service-to-service communication.
*   **Termination:** TLS terminates at the edge reverse proxy (e.g., Traefik or Nginx). mTLS is enforced by the service mesh (e.g., Istio or Linkerd) for internal traffic.
*   **Zero-Trust:** No plaintext HTTP anywhere in the cluster.

### 5.4 Deployment Targets
*   **Production:** `k8s-prod.corp.internal` (5 nodes, multi-AZ).
*   **Staging:** `k8s-stg.corp.internal` (single-region).
*   **Development:** Docker Compose on developer laptops (Windows/Ubuntu). Must replicate K8s networking (mTLS, Vault injection) as closely as possible.

## 6. Observability & Logging

### 6.1 Metrics
*   **System:** Prometheus.
*   **Instrumentation:** Use the Python Prometheus client library. Expose standard metrics (HTTP request duration, error rates, queue depth) and custom metrics (sync batch size, encryption latency).

### 6.2 Distributed Tracing
*   **System:** Tempo.
*   **Propagation:** Trace IDs are injected into logs via `company-common-logging` and propagated in HTTP headers between services.

### 6.3 Logging & Audit
*   **Application Logs:** Structured JSON to Loki via `company-common-logging`.
*   **Audit Log:**
    *   **Format:** `audit-format-v3` (actor_id, action, target_id, target_classification, timestamp_utc).
    *   **Sink:** Dedicated Loki stream with indefinite retention.
    *   **Trigger:** Generated by the backend on every write action (create/update/delete). The client does not generate the canonical audit log.

## 7. CI/CD Pipeline

*   **System:** GitLab CI.
*   **Pipeline:** Defined in `.gitlab-ci.yml`.
*   **Staging:** Automatic deployment on merge to `main`.
*   **Production:** Manual approval gate by platform leads.
*   **Build:**
    *   Pulls base images from Artifactory.
    *   Installs dependencies from Artifactory PyPI mirror.
    *   Runs tests and linting.
    *   Builds and pushes images to Artifactory.

## 8. Timezone Handling

*   **Storage:** All timestamps in PostgreSQL and audit logs are in UTC.
*   **Display:** The client displays timestamps in the user’s local timezone, derived from the Keycloak profile’s `zoneinfo` claim. The API returns UTC timestamps; the client is responsible for conversion.

## 9. Risk Mitigation & Open Items

*   **Latency Risk:** p99 < 200ms is a hard constraint. Monitor database query performance closely. Consider connection pooling (PgBouncer) if the managed PG does not handle high concurrency efficiently.
*   **Sync Complexity:** Conflict resolution for offline data is complex. Define detailed conflict resolution rules in the product spec.
*   **Key Rotation:** Local encryption key rotation is a significant UX challenge. Define the flow for key rotation in the security brief.
*   **Base Image SLA:** Account for the 1-week mirror SLA in the project timeline.

This architecture adheres to all constraints and provides a robust, compliant, and performant foundation for the FieldOps rebuild.
