# FieldOps — Product & Team Context

## Why we are rebuilding

FieldOps is the internal tooling used by our field operations team —
surveyors, drillers, inspectors — across roughly 260 users. The current
platform is a VB.NET tool first shipped in 2011, then patched heavily
through three different vendor handovers. By 2023 the codebase had
accumulated about fourteen years of architectural debt and nobody on the
current internal team can reliably extend it without breaking something
else. The 2024 "billing cycle" outage — where a patch to the timesheet
export broke the inbound photo ingest — cost the team four days of field
capture. That was the trigger. Engineering leadership signed off on a
rewrite in Q4 2024; target launch is Q3 of next year with a soft internal
rollout to two regional teams first, then full cutover by Q1 of the year
after.

## Who actually uses it

The field team is not a software team. They use laptops as tools. The
central office issues ThinkPad X1 Carbons running Windows 11 Pro — that
is the default, and the one most users run. The regional offices in the
western territory standardized on Dell XPS 13 laptops running Ubuntu
22.04 LTS, because the local IT lead at the time preferred open-source
and won that argument back in 2021. Procurement is not going to undo
that; both platforms are permanent. A Mac request came up during the
2023 planning round from the analytics group, who wanted to use the data
export from their own MacBooks; that request was declined by IT because
the procurement contract doesn't include Apple hardware and the
compliance desk doesn't want to certify a third client platform. Mac is
not a target. Any proposal that plans for Mac support is planning for
work we will not staff.

Most of our users spend two to five days in the office in a cycle, then
multi-week stretches in remote locations — offshore rigs, mountain
passes, rural transmission corridors, desert survey lines. In those
locations the connection is either expensive satellite (high-latency,
metered), intermittent LTE (usable only in the morning hours when a
distant tower has capacity), or entirely absent for days. Our own
internal survey of field laptops across Q2 2024 found a mean
connectivity availability of 31% of the working day, with the 5th
percentile at 0%. The platform must let field staff do their full day
offline and reconcile whenever the laptop reaches a known-good network
(office Wi-Fi, hotel Wi-Fi on a travel day, regional office on a
stopover). We are not shipping a design where the client requires an
open connection to the server during field work. That is a non-starter.

## Developer team

The backend team is five engineers: three of them built our previous two
Python services (the permit-intake service and the asset-catalog
service), and they have asked that we standardize on Python going
forward. Our build images are on Python 3.11.6 in production and the
team wants to use the newer match-statement and exception-group
features. We are not downgrading Python to 3.9 or 3.10 to match some
external library — pin the library, not the runtime. Front-end is one
engineer plus a contractor; they use TypeScript and the choice of UI
framework is being made separately and is not in scope for the
architecture proposal.

## Performance expectations

Users capture data at 1-second cadence for certain field surveys, and
the existing tool's 3–4 second save latency is the single most common
complaint in our user-satisfaction survey. For the rebuild, the product
manager has made p99 server-side latency under 200 milliseconds a hard
acceptance criterion — this is written into the sign-off documentation,
not a stretch goal. Meeting this is non-negotiable; if an architectural
choice pushes latency above 200ms p99, pick a different choice.

## Image distribution

All our service container images live in our internal JFrog Artifactory
at `artifactory.corp.internal/docker/`. Public Docker Hub is blocked at
the corporate egress firewall — builds that reference `python:3.11-slim`
or `postgres:15-alpine` from Docker Hub will fail in CI because the
builder image cannot reach Docker Hub. Every base image we use must be
mirrored into Artifactory first, and the mirror process runs weekly.
This is a policy from the 2023 supply-chain audit and it is not moving.
So the architecture needs to specify its base images in terms of the
internal mirror — and if a new base image is needed, the platform team
has a ~1-week SLA on adding it to the Artifactory mirror, which the
project timeline must accommodate.

## What we are building

The core of the system is a record-of-work database: field staff capture
observations, photos, and structured measurements on the laptop; the
client reconciles offline captures on reconnect; findings are submitted
up the chain to the central operations team; the central team reviews,
annotates, and either finalizes the record or sends it back to the
field. The system has a web portal for the central team, a thick-client
desktop app for the field team, and an API surface for a handful of
downstream systems (the billing system, the asset catalog, the
compliance desk's audit tools).

## Related briefs

You will write the architecture proposal. Before drafting, read the
infrastructure brief (database, network, deployment, container policy,
queueing) and the security-and-compliance brief (identity, data
classification, storage, audit). Specifics in those briefs bind your
proposal — there are a number of hard constraints and several
anti-patterns to avoid.

# FieldOps — Infrastructure Constraints

## Data tier

After the May 2024 incident — a pathological MySQL 8 query-planner
regression during a failover that took out the permit-intake service
for six hours — engineering leadership standardized the new stack on
PostgreSQL. The platform team runs managed PostgreSQL clusters for two
other internal products (permit-intake on PG 15.4, asset-catalog on PG
15.6) and they have capacity for FieldOps on the same managed tier. The
sign-off is conditional: we stay on **PostgreSQL 15 or newer**. The
managed tier's automation chain (backup scheduling, PITR, extension
management) only supports PG 15+ and a separate tier for an older
version is not in the budget. Proposals assuming MySQL, SQLite as the
primary server-side store, MongoDB, or any document database will need
to be argued against this baseline — which is a fight not worth having.
For the local client store (offline-first), SQLite on the laptop is
fine; that's client-side, not the server data tier.

## Network plane

All traffic — client-to-server AND service-to-service within the
cluster — runs over TLS. The corporate zero-trust project that ran
through 2024 established "no plaintext HTTP anywhere inside the
cluster" as a hard baseline, and the security review at launch will
block any service that breaks this. TLS terminates at the reverse proxy
at the edge, and then mTLS between services internally. This is
enforced by service-mesh policy in production. If your proposal shows
"internal HTTP between the API and the worker" as a quick shortcut,
expect the launch to be blocked.

## Container registry

Public Docker Hub is blocked at the corporate egress firewall. All base
images pull from our internal Artifactory mirror at
`artifactory.corp.internal/docker/`. We don't get to use `FROM
python:3.11-slim` directly — it has to be
`FROM artifactory.corp.internal/docker/python:3.11-slim`. The same
applies to Postgres, Redis (if we used it — see below), any Node image,
any Alpine base image. The platform team's mirror adds new images on a
~1-week SLA, so plan base-image changes in advance. This is a post-2023
supply-chain-audit policy and it is not flexible.

## Secrets management

All service secrets live in our HashiCorp Vault deployment at
`vault.corp.internal`. Applications authenticate to Vault via Kubernetes
service-account JWT, then pull secrets at startup. We do not use
Kubernetes Secrets directly for sensitive material — the compliance desk
has ruled that as insufficient protection. We do not put secrets in
environment variables at deploy time, and we do not put them in config
files. The pattern is: Vault Agent injects secrets into the pod's tmpfs
at startup, and the application reads them there. 12-factor orthodoxy
about env-var secrets does not apply here — compliance trumps it.

## Queueing and async work

We do NOT have Redis in production, and we are not adding it for this
project. The platform team ran Redis for a year (2022) and hit enough
operational pain — memory-fragmentation eviction, replication lag,
authorization gotchas — that they standardized on PostgreSQL as the
queue backend for async work. The pattern we use is the
`postgres-listen-notify` plus a claimable-task pattern in a dedicated
jobs table with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`. Performance has been adequate
for permit-intake (~2k jobs/hour peak) and for asset-catalog (~400
jobs/hour steady). Unless FieldOps workloads demand >10k jobs/hour
sustained — which the current estimates don't — use the same
PostgreSQL-as-queue pattern. Don't propose Redis, RabbitMQ, SQS, NATS,
or any other dedicated message broker. The platform team will push
back.

## Idempotence and delivery semantics

All background jobs must be idempotent and assume at-least-once
delivery. We've been burned twice by "exactly-once" claims (once in the
old Redis setup, once in a short-lived Kafka experiment in 2023) and
the team's policy is now: design for at-least-once, assert idempotence
in code, test by submitting each job twice in staging. The architecture
proposal needs to say what the idempotence keys are for each background
job type.

## Deployment targets

Production runs on our internal Kubernetes platform
(`k8s-prod.corp.internal`, five nodes, multi-AZ). Staging is a smaller
single-region cluster on `k8s-stg.corp.internal`. Local development uses
Docker Compose on developer laptops; since the backend developers
include both Windows 11 (Docker Desktop) and Ubuntu 22.04 (Docker
Engine) users, any dev-environment helper scripts must work on both.

## Observability

Metrics go to our existing Prometheus cluster. Distributed traces go to
Tempo. Logs go to Loki. Do not propose Datadog, New Relic, Honeycomb,
or any alternate stack — the platform team runs Prometheus/Tempo/Loki
and the cost budget for this program does not include a bespoke
observability vendor.

## CI/CD

The CI/CD system is GitLab CI. Pipelines are defined per-repo via
`.gitlab-ci.yml`. Deployments to staging are automatic on merge to
`main`; production deployments are gated on a manual approval by one of
the two platform leads. Don't propose a GitHub Actions-based pipeline —
the repos live in our self-hosted GitLab.

# FieldOps — Security & Compliance

## Identity

The compliance desk has reviewed this program and approved use of our
self-hosted Keycloak deployment at `keycloak.corp.internal` as the
identity plane. Two other FieldOps-adjacent tools already federate into
that Keycloak — the permit-intake service and the asset-catalog
service — and the realm, roles, and group structure are already in
place. External identity providers — Auth0, Okta, Google Workspace as
an IdP, Azure AD, Cognito, Firebase Authentication, any managed SSO —
are NOT approved for this program. The compliance reasoning: field data
includes client-site geolocation traces and asset photographs that
were scoped under contract as data-in-our-custody, and the contract
negotiation explicitly ruled out routing identity claims through a
third-party SaaS. Do not propose any of those third-party IdPs as a
fallback, as a staging shortcut, or as a "for local dev only"
convenience. The dev environment federates into the same Keycloak via
VPN.

If a future program wants to re-evaluate third-party identity that will
be a separate compliance engagement. Out of scope here.

## Photo and attachment storage

Captured photos and attachments are stored in an S3-compatible object
store — specifically, our internal MinIO deployment at
`objects.corp.internal`. Every object must be written with AES-256
server-side encryption (SSE-S3 equivalent, using the MinIO-managed key
hierarchy). We do not store media files on the application pod's local
filesystem, we do not store them in PostgreSQL as bytea, and we do not
route them through a separate cloud provider's object store. The MinIO
deployment is what we have; use it. Inline references to objects go in
the PostgreSQL row as canonical URIs like `s3://fieldops/<capture-id>/
<asset-id>`.

## Data classification

Most captured data is Internal classification. A small subset — the
geolocation traces for restricted client sites — is Confidential. The
platform must tag a record as Confidential at capture time and route it
through a stricter retention and access path. The storage backend is
the same (same PostgreSQL cluster, same MinIO bucket); differentiation
is enforced at the application layer against Keycloak roles. A user
without the `fieldops.confidential` role should get a 403 on read
attempts for Confidential records, logged to the audit trail.

## Audit log

Every write action must be logged to an append-only audit log. The
audit format is `audit-format-v3` — already defined in the internal
wiki by the compliance desk, and it is the canonical format across our
services. Do not invent a different format; do not use
event-sourcing-style JSON payloads with bespoke fields; do not propose
a custom "better" schema. The compliance team reads the audit log
quarterly and they consume `audit-format-v3` with their existing tools.
The format's key fields include actor_id (Keycloak user_id), action
verb, target_id, target_classification, and a monotonic timestamp in
UTC. The audit log sink is a dedicated Loki stream with long retention
(see below).

## Logging

All application logging uses our internal `company-common-logging`
Python library, not stdlib `logging` directly and not `loguru` or
`structlog`. The company-common-logging library wraps stdlib logging
with our required fields (trace_id injection from Tempo, service
identity from the env, structured JSON output for Loki). Every Python
service at this company uses this library, which is how Loki/Tempo
correlation works — if you propose stdlib logging or a third-party
logging library, trace correlation will silently break and the on-call
dashboards won't work. It is installed as
`company-common-logging @ artifactory.corp.internal/pypi/`.

## Transport

See the infrastructure brief for TLS posture: all channels TLS
end-to-end, no plaintext internal HTTP, mTLS between internal services.

## Offline capture & at-rest encryption

Because the client works offline, the on-device store holds some
Confidential data between sync cycles. The device store is encrypted
at rest. Key material is derived from the user's Keycloak session — so
when a user rotates out of the program (access revoked in Keycloak),
the keys are unusable on any laptop they previously held. Specifics of
the KDF will be defined in a follow-up brief; for this architecture
proposal, treat "local store encrypted at rest with keys derived from
Keycloak session identity" as a binding requirement. The local SQLite
file on the laptop is encrypted at rest.

## Time and timezone

All timestamps stored in PostgreSQL and in the audit log are in UTC.
The client displays timestamps in the user's local timezone (derived
from the Keycloak profile's `zoneinfo` claim), never in server TZ,
never in "whatever the laptop clock says." UTC-in-storage,
local-TZ-for-display: write it this way and be explicit about it in
the API layer, because every previous project here has bungled
timezone handling at least once.

## Data retention

Captured field records (rows plus media objects) are retained for 7
years from capture date, then hard-deleted with tombstone rows
preserving the record ID and classification. The audit log is retained
indefinitely — it is the system of record for who did what, and
compliance requires it be kept. Do not propose "retain everything
forever" or "7-year retention on everything including audit"; the
split is deliberate.

## Out of scope

Red-team penetration testing is scheduled for pre-launch. Not a
concern for the architecture proposal.

**Context:** FieldOps Rewrite Architecture Proposal
**Status:** Pre-proposal / Constraint Mapping

## 1. Executive Summary of Constraints
The architecture is heavily constrained by **legacy infrastructure realities** and **strict compliance policies**. We are not building a greenfield cloud-native ideal; we are building a robust, offline-first, Python/PostgreSQL/MinIO system on a specific internal Kubernetes platform. The primary tension lies in balancing the **offline-first client requirement** (high latency tolerance, local storage) with the **server-side performance SLA** (p99 < 200ms) and **zero-trust security** (mTLS, Vault, Keycloak).

    *   *Constraint:* Do **not** downgrade Python to support external libraries. Pin libraries to compatible versions.

    *   *Constraint:* UI framework choice is **out of scope** for this architecture proposal. Do not propose a specific framework (React/Angular/etc.). Focus on API contract and data flow.

    *   *Constraint:* Client-side offline store **can** use SQLite.
2.  **Async Queueing:** PostgreSQL-only.
    *   *Constraint:* **No Redis, RabbitMQ, SQS, NATS.**
    *   *Pattern:* `LISTEN/NOTIFY` + Claimable Task Table (`FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`).
    *   *Capacity Check:* Current estimates do not exceed 10k jobs/hour. If they do, this constraint becomes a blocker, but current specs say "adequate."
3.  **Object Storage:** Internal MinIO (`objects.corp.internal`).
    *   *Constraint:* S3-compatible API.
    *   *Constraint:* AES-256 Server-Side Encryption (SSE-S3/MinIO-managed key).
    *   *Constraint:* No local filesystem storage for media. No `bytea` in PG.

4.  **Data Classification & Retention:**
    *   *Classification:* `Internal` (default) vs. `Confidential` (geolocation traces).
    *   *Enforcement:* Application-layer role check (`fieldops.confidential`) against Keycloak. 403 on unauthorized access.
    *   *Retention:* Field records = 7 years (hard delete + tombstone). Audit log = Indefinite.

### C. Security & Identity Constraints (Hard)
1.  **Identity Provider:** Self-hosted Keycloak (`keycloak.corp.internal`).
    *   *Constraint:* **No Auth0, Okta, Azure AD, Cognito, Firebase.**
    *   *Constraint:* No third-party IdP for dev/staging either. Dev env uses VPN to Keycloak.
    *   *Integration:* Federates with existing Permit-Intake and Asset-Catalog realms.
2.  **Secrets Management:** HashiCorp Vault (`vault.corp.internal`).
    *   *Constraint:* **No Kubernetes Secrets** for sensitive data. **No Env Vars** for secrets at deploy time.
    *   *Pattern:* Vault Agent injects secrets into pod `tmpfs` at startup. App reads from file.
3.  **Network & Transport:**
    *   *Constraint:* **Zero Trust.** No plaintext HTTP anywhere (internal or external).
    *   *Edge:* TLS termination at Reverse Proxy.
    *   *Internal:* mTLS between all services (enforced by Service Mesh).
4.  **Offline Client Security:**
    *   *Constraint:* Local SQLite store encrypted at rest.
    *   *Key Derivation:* Keys derived from Keycloak session identity.
    *   *Revocation:* If Keycloak access is revoked, local keys become unusable (cryptographic unlinking).

### D. Observability & Logging Constraints (Hard)
1.  **Logging Library:** `company-common-logging` (Python).
    *   *Constraint:* **No stdlib `logging`, `loguru`, `structlog`.**
    *   *Requirement:* Must inject `trace_id` from Tempo. Must output structured JSON for Loki.
    *   *Source:* Installed from `artifactory.corp.internal/pypi/`.
2.  **Audit Log:**
    *   *Format:* `audit-format-v3` (Canonical).
    *   *Fields:* `actor_id`, `action`, `target_id`, `target_classification`, `timestamp` (UTC).
    *   *Sink:* Dedicated Loki stream with long retention.
    *   *Constraint:* Do not invent custom schemas.
3.  **Metrics/Traces:** Prometheus (Metrics), Tempo (Traces), Loki (Logs).
    *   *Constraint:* No Datadog, New Relic, Honeycomb.

### E. Performance & Latency Constraints (Hard)
1.  **Server-Side Latency:** p99 < 200ms.
    *   *Constraint:* Non-negotiable acceptance criterion.
    *   *Implication:* Architectural choices that add network hops, complex serialization, or heavy ORM overhead must be rejected or optimized aggressively.
2.  **Client-Side Cadence:** 1-second capture interval.
    *   *Implication:* Client must handle high-frequency local writes without blocking UI. Sync logic must be efficient (delta-based, not full-replace).
3.  **Offline-First Requirement:**
    *   *Constraint:* Full functionality offline. Reconciliation only on "known-good" network.
    *   *Implication:* Client must have robust conflict resolution strategy. Server must handle out-of-order or duplicate submissions gracefully (idempotence).

### F. Deployment & CI/CD Constraints (Hard)
1.  **Infrastructure:** Internal Kubernetes (`k8s-prod.corp.internal`, 5 nodes, multi-AZ).
2.  **CI/CD:** GitLab CI (`.gitlab-ci.yml`).
    *   *Constraint:* No GitHub Actions.
3.  **Dev Environment:** Docker Compose.
    *   *Constraint:* Must work on Windows 11 (Docker Desktop) AND Ubuntu 22.04 (Docker Engine). Cross-platform compatibility for dev scripts is required.

---

## 3. Tensions & Trade-offs Identified

### Tension 1: Offline-First Complexity vs. Server Latency SLA
*   **The Conflict:** The client must store 1-second cadence data locally and sync later. The server must process these syncs with p99 < 200ms.
*   **Risk:** If the sync process involves complex validation, heavy ORM queries, or external API calls during the sync window, the p99 latency will be breached.
*   **Architectural Implication:** Sync logic must be lightweight on the server. Likely requires a dedicated "ingestion" endpoint that is fast and dumb (write to queue/DB immediately), with heavy validation happening asynchronously in the background (using the PG queue pattern). The 200ms SLA likely applies to the *acknowledgment* of the sync, not the final processing of the data.

### Tension 2: PostgreSQL Queueing vs. High-Frequency Syncs
*   **The Conflict:** We are using `LISTEN/NOTIFY` + `SKIP LOCKED` for async work. FieldOps has high-frequency data capture (1/sec). When a user reconnects, they may have thousands of records to sync.
*   **Risk:** If the sync process creates one job per record, we might overwhelm the PG queue or the workers. If we batch them, we risk losing the "at-least-once" guarantee if a batch fails partially.
*   **Architectural Implication:** Need a "Batch Sync" job type. The client sends a batch of records; the server creates *one* job to process the batch. Idempotence keys must be at the batch level or individual record level within the batch.

### Tension 3: Zero-Trust/mTLS vs. Offline Client
*   **The Conflict:** Internal services require mTLS. The client is offline and cannot maintain mTLS certificates with the server during offline periods.
*   **Resolution:** mTLS is for *service-to-service* communication. The client-to-server communication is TLS (standard). The constraint "no plaintext HTTP anywhere" applies to the *network plane*. The client uses standard TLS (likely client certs or API keys managed via Keycloak), but the *internal* service mesh enforces mTLS.
*   **Clarification Needed:** How does the offline client authenticate? It likely uses a JWT from Keycloak (obtained when online) for API auth, not mTLS. The mTLS constraint applies to the backend services (API -> Worker -> DB).

### Tension 4: Confidential Data Encryption vs. Offline Access
*   **The Conflict:** Confidential data must be encrypted at rest on the device, with keys derived from Keycloak session.
*   **Risk:** If the user's Keycloak session expires or is revoked while offline, they cannot access their data. If they come back online and the session is revoked, the data is cryptographically locked.
*   **Architectural Implication:** The client must handle "key rotation" or "session refresh" gracefully. The architecture must define how the client obtains the initial encryption key (from Keycloak) and how it handles the case where the session is no longer valid (e.g., prompt to re-authenticate, which requires network).

### Tension 5: Python 3.11 Features vs. Library Compatibility
*   **The Conflict:** Team wants to use Python 3.11 features (`match`, `exception-group`). Some libraries might not support 3.11 or might require older versions.
*   **Risk:** Being forced to use older Python versions or pin libraries to incompatible versions.
*   **Architectural Implication:** Strict library vetting. Only use libraries that support Python 3.11. If a critical library doesn't, it must be replaced or forked.

---

## 4. Open Questions & Ambiguities

1.  **Sync Conflict Resolution Strategy:**
    *   *Question:* How are conflicts resolved? (Last-write-wins? Server-authoritative? Manual review?)
    *   *Impact:* Affects data model (version vectors? timestamps?) and client logic.
2.  **Batch Size for Sync:**
    *   *Question:* What is the maximum batch size a client can send?
    *   *Impact:* Affects payload size limits, queue job size, and processing time.
3.  **Keycloak Session Lifetime for Offline Use:**
    *   *Question:* How long does a Keycloak session last? How does the client refresh it offline?
    *   *Impact:* Determines how long a user can work offline before needing to reconnect to Keycloak.
4.  **Audit Log Volume:**
    *   *Question:* What is the expected volume of audit logs?
    *   *Impact:* Loki retention and storage costs. (Though retention is indefinite, cost might be a concern).
5.  **Dev Environment Keycloak/Vault:**
    *   *Question:* How do developers get Keycloak and Vault in their local Docker Compose setup?
    *   *Impact:* Dev experience complexity. Do we mock these services or run them locally?
6.  **Photo Upload Latency:**
    *   *Question:* Are photos synced in the same batch as text data?
    *   *Impact:* Large payloads might breach the 200ms p99 SLA if not handled asynchronously.
7.  **Timezone Handling in Client:**
    *   *Question:* How does the client get the user's timezone?
    *   *Impact:* Client must fetch `zoneinfo` from Keycloak profile. What if it's missing? Fallback?
8.  **Idempotence Key Generation:**
    *   *Question:* Who generates the idempotence key for each job?
    *   *Impact:* Client must generate unique IDs for each offline action. Server must validate uniqueness.

---

## 5. Proposed Architecture Direction (Mental Draft)

*   **Client:** Thick Desktop App (Electron/Tauri? - *Out of scope for framework, but implies local SQLite + Encryption*).
    *   Offline: Local SQLite (encrypted).
    *   Online: Syncs via REST API (TLS).
    *   Auth: JWT from Keycloak.
*   **API Gateway:** Reverse Proxy (TLS termination).
*   **Backend Services:**
    *   Python 3.11.
    *   FastAPI or similar (lightweight for p99).
    *   mTLS with other services.
    *   Secrets from Vault (tmpfs).
    *   Logging: `company-common-logging`.
*   **Data Layer:**
    *   PostgreSQL 15+ (Managed).
    *   MinIO (Object Storage).
    *   Queue: PG `LISTEN/NOTIFY` + Task Table.
*   **Infrastructure:**
    *   K8s (Internal).
    *   GitLab CI.
    *   Prometheus/Tempo/Loki.

---

## 6. Next Steps for Proposal Writer

1.  **Define API Contract:** Focus on the sync endpoint. How does the client send data? How does the server acknowledge?
2.  **Detail Offline Sync Logic:** How does the client handle conflicts? How does it encrypt/decrypt?
3.  **Specify Idempotence Strategy:** Define the idempotence key format for each job type.
4.  **Address Latency:** Explain how the 200ms p99 SLA is met (e.g., async processing, caching, optimized queries).
5.  **Address Security:** Detail Keycloak integration, Vault usage, and MinIO encryption.
6.  **Address Dev/Deploy:** Detail Docker Compose setup for dev, GitLab CI pipeline structure.
7.  **Address Compliance:** Detail audit log format, data retention, and classification handling.

**Critical Warning:** Do not propose any technology outside the specified stack (Python 3.11, PG 15+, MinIO, Keycloak, Vault, Prometheus/Tempo/Loki, GitLab CI, K8s). Do not propose Mac support. Do not propose Redis. Do not propose Docker Hub.

# FieldOps Rebuild: Technical Architecture Proposal

## 1. Executive Summary

This proposal defines the architecture for the FieldOps rebuild, replacing the legacy VB.NET system with a modern, offline-first, Python-based platform. The design prioritizes three non-negotiable constraints: **offline resilience** for field staff in low-connectivity environments, **p99 server-side latency under 200ms**, and strict adherence to internal security and infrastructure policies (Zero Trust, Vault, Keycloak, MinIO). The system consists of a thick-client desktop application for Windows 11 and Ubuntu 22.04, a Python 3.11 backend, and a PostgreSQL 15+ data tier.

## 2. Platform & Runtime

### Backend Services
*   **Language:** Python 3.11.6. We leverage `match` statements and `exception-group` features. No downgrades to 3.9/3.10 are permitted.
*   **Framework:** FastAPI. Chosen for its low overhead and async capabilities, critical for meeting the 200ms p99 latency SLA.
*   **Base Image:** `FROM artifactory.corp.internal/docker/python:3.11-slim`. Docker Hub is blocked; all images must be mirrored internally.
*   **Logging:** `company-common-logging` library, installed from `artifactory.corp.internal/pypi/`. This ensures trace_id injection from Tempo and structured JSON output for Loki. Stdlib `logging` is prohibited.

### Client Application
*   **Runtime:** Electron (or Tauri, subject to frontend framework decision) targeting Windows 11 Pro and Ubuntu 22.04 LTS.
*   **Exclusions:** macOS is explicitly out of scope.
*   **Local Storage:** SQLite database, encrypted at rest.
*   **Encryption:** Keys derived from the user’s Keycloak session identity. If access is revoked in Keycloak, local keys become cryptographically invalid.

## 3. Database & Storage

### Primary Data Store
*   **Technology:** PostgreSQL 15 (Managed Tier).
*   **Version:** PG 15.4 or newer. MySQL, MongoDB, and document DBs are excluded.
*   **Schema Strategy:** Relational schema with strict typing. All timestamps stored in UTC.
*   **Retention:** Field records retained for 7 years (hard delete + tombstone). Audit logs retained indefinitely.

### Object Storage
*   **Technology:** Internal MinIO (`objects.corp.internal`).
*   **Protocol:** S3-compatible API.
*   **Encryption:** AES-256 Server-Side Encryption (SSE-S3/MinIO-managed keys).
*   **Reference:** Media URIs stored in PostgreSQL as `s3://fieldops/<capture-id>/<asset-id>`. No `bytea` columns. No local filesystem storage for media.

### Async Queueing
*   **Technology:** PostgreSQL-native queueing.
*   **Pattern:** `LISTEN/NOTIFY` combined with a claimable task table using `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`.
*   **Rationale:** Redis, RabbitMQ, and SQS are excluded. This pattern supports the estimated workload (<10k jobs/hour) and aligns with platform standards.
*   **Idempotence:** All jobs are idempotent. Idempotence keys are defined per job type (e.g., `sync_batch_id`, `photo_upload_id`) and stored in the task table. Jobs are designed for at-least-once delivery; duplicate processing is handled via unique constraints and idempotent logic.

## 4. Identity & Security

### Identity Provider
*   **Technology:** Self-hosted Keycloak (`keycloak.corp.internal`).
*   **Integration:** Federates with existing Permit-Intake and Asset-Catalog realms.
*   **Exclusions:** No Auth0, Okta, Azure AD, or Cognito. No third-party IdPs for dev/staging. Dev environment uses VPN to access Keycloak.
*   **Roles:** `fieldops.confidential` role controls access to restricted geolocation data. Unauthorized access attempts return 403 and are logged.

### Secrets Management
*   **Technology:** HashiCorp Vault (`vault.corp.internal`).
*   **Pattern:** Kubernetes Service Account JWT authentication. Vault Agent injects secrets into pod `tmpfs` at startup.
*   **Exclusions:** No Kubernetes Secrets for sensitive data. No environment variable secrets at deploy time.

### Transport & Network
*   **Policy:** Zero Trust. No plaintext HTTP anywhere.
*   **Edge:** TLS termination at the reverse proxy.
*   **Internal:** mTLS between all services, enforced by the service mesh.
*   **Client Auth:** JWT from Keycloak for API authentication.

## 5. Offline & Sync Strategy

### Client-Side Offline
*   **Storage:** Encrypted SQLite on device.
*   **Capture:** 1-second cadence data is written locally immediately. UI remains responsive.
*   **Timezone:** Client displays timestamps in user’s local timezone (from Keycloak `zoneinfo` claim). All stored timestamps are UTC.

### Sync Mechanism
*   **Trigger:** Sync occurs when the client detects a "known-good" network (office/hotel Wi-Fi).
*   **Batching:** Client batches offline changes into a single payload to reduce network overhead.
*   **Server-Side Processing:**
    1.  API endpoint receives batch, validates JWT, and returns 202 Accepted within 200ms p99.
    2.  Batch is enqueued as a single job in PostgreSQL.
    3.  Worker processes the batch asynchronously, writing to PostgreSQL and MinIO.
    4.  Audit logs are generated in `audit-format-v3` format.
*   **Conflict Resolution:** Server-authoritative. Last-write-wins based on UTC timestamp. Conflicts are logged but not automatically resolved by the client.

## 6. Observability & Logging

### Metrics & Tracing
*   **Metrics:** Prometheus. Custom metrics for sync latency, queue depth, and error rates.
*   **Tracing:** Tempo. Distributed traces injected via `company-common-logging`.
*   **Logs:** Loki. Structured JSON logs from `company-common-logging`.

### Audit Log
*   **Format:** `audit-format-v3`.
*   **Fields:** `actor_id` (Keycloak user_id), `action`, `target_id`, `target_classification`, `timestamp` (UTC).
*   **Sink:** Dedicated Loki stream with indefinite retention.

## 7. Deployment & CI/CD

### Infrastructure
*   **Production:** Internal Kubernetes (`k8s-prod.corp.internal`, 5 nodes, multi-AZ).
*   **Staging:** `k8s-stg.corp.internal`.
*   **Dev:** Docker Compose on Windows 11 and Ubuntu 22.04. Scripts must be cross-platform compatible.

### CI/CD
*   **System:** GitLab CI (`.gitlab-ci.yml`).
*   **Pipeline:**
    1.  **Build:** Pull base images from `artifactory.corp.internal/docker/`.
    2.  **Test:** Unit and integration tests.
    3.  **Deploy to Staging:** Automatic on merge to `main`.
    4.  **Deploy to Production:** Manual approval by platform lead.
*   **Image Registry:** `artifactory.corp.internal/docker/`.

### Container Images
*   **Base Images:** All `FROM` statements reference `artifactory.corp.internal/docker/`.
*   **Postgres:** `artifactory.corp.internal/docker/postgres:15-alpine`.
*   **MinIO:** `artifactory.corp.internal/docker/minio:latest`.
*   **Keycloak/Vault:** Managed externally; not part of FieldOps container images.

## 8. Timezone Handling

*   **Storage:** All timestamps in PostgreSQL and audit logs are UTC.
*   **API:** All API responses include UTC timestamps.
*   **Client:** Client fetches user’s timezone from Keycloak profile (`zoneinfo` claim) and converts UTC timestamps to local time for display.
*   **Validation:** Server rejects timestamps with ambiguous or missing timezone info.

## 9. Data Classification & Retention

*   **Classification:** `Internal` (default) and `Confidential` (geolocation traces).
*   **Enforcement:** Application-layer check against Keycloak role `fieldops.confidential`.
*   **Retention:**
    *   Field Records: 7 years. Hard delete with tombstone row.
    *   Audit Logs: Indefinite.

## 10. Conclusion

This architecture adheres strictly to all constraints: Python 3.11, PostgreSQL 15+, MinIO, Keycloak, Vault, Prometheus/Tempo/Loki, and GitLab CI. # FieldOps — Product & Team Context

## Why we are rebuilding

FieldOps is the internal tooling used by our field operations team —
surveyors, drillers, inspectors — across roughly 260 users. The current
platform is a VB.NET tool first shipped in 2011, then patched heavily
through three different vendor handovers. By 2023 the codebase had
accumulated about fourteen years of architectural debt and nobody on the
current internal team can reliably extend it without breaking something
else. The 2024 "billing cycle" outage — where a patch to the timesheet
export broke the inbound photo ingest — cost the team four days of field
capture. That was the trigger. Engineering leadership signed off on a
rewrite in Q4 2024; target launch is Q3 of next year with a soft internal
rollout to two regional teams first, then full cutover by Q1 of the year
after.

## Who actually uses it

The field team is not a software team. They use laptops as tools. The
central office issues ThinkPad X1 Carbons running Windows 11 Pro — that
is the default, and the one most users run. The regional offices in the
western territory standardized on Dell XPS 13 laptops running Ubuntu
22.04 LTS, because the local IT lead at the time preferred open-source
and won that argument back in 2021. Procurement is not going to undo
that; both platforms are permanent. A Mac request came up during the
2023 planning round from the analytics group, who wanted to use the data
export from their own MacBooks; that request was declined by IT because
the procurement contract doesn't include Apple hardware and the
compliance desk doesn't want to certify a third client platform. Mac is
not a target. Any proposal that plans for Mac support is planning for
work we will not staff.

Most of our users spend two to five days in the office in a cycle, then
multi-week stretches in remote locations — offshore rigs, mountain
passes, rural transmission corridors, desert survey lines. In those
locations the connection is either expensive satellite (high-latency,
metered), intermittent LTE (usable only in the morning hours when a
distant tower has capacity), or entirely absent for days. Our own
internal survey of field laptops across Q2 2024 found a mean
connectivity availability of 31% of the working day, with the 5th
percentile at 0%. The platform must let field staff do their full day
offline and reconcile whenever the laptop reaches a known-good network
(office Wi-Fi, hotel Wi-Fi on a travel day, regional office on a
stopover). We are not shipping a design where the client requires an
open connection to the server during field work. That is a non-starter.

## Developer team

The backend team is five engineers: three of them built our previous two
Python services (the permit-intake service and the asset-catalog
service), and they have asked that we standardize on Python going
forward. Our build images are on Python 3.11.6 in production and the
team wants to use the newer match-statement and exception-group
features. We are not downgrading Python to 3.9 or 3.10 to match some
external library — pin the library, not the runtime. Front-end is one
engineer plus a contractor; they use TypeScript and the choice of UI
framework is being made separately and is not in scope for the
architecture proposal.

## Performance expectations

Users capture data at 1-second cadence for certain field surveys, and
the existing tool's 3–4 second save latency is the single most common
complaint in our user-satisfaction survey. For the rebuild, the product
manager has made p99 server-side latency under 200 milliseconds a hard
acceptance criterion — this is written into the sign-off documentation,
not a stretch goal. Meeting this is non-negotiable; if an architectural
choice pushes latency above 200ms p99, pick a different choice.

## Image distribution

All our service container images live in our internal JFrog Artifactory
at `artifactory.corp.internal/docker/`. Public Docker Hub is blocked at
the corporate egress firewall — builds that reference `python:3.11-slim`
or `postgres:15-alpine` from Docker Hub will fail in CI because the
builder image cannot reach Docker Hub. Every base image we use must be
mirrored into Artifactory first, and the mirror process runs weekly.
This is a policy from the 2023 supply-chain audit and it is not moving.
So the architecture needs to specify its base images in terms of the
internal mirror — and if a new base image is needed, the platform team
has a ~1-week SLA on adding it to the Artifactory mirror, which the
project timeline must accommodate.

## What we are building

The core of the system is a record-of-work database: field staff capture
observations, photos, and structured measurements on the laptop; the
client reconciles offline captures on reconnect; findings are submitted
up the chain to the central operations team; the central team reviews,
annotates, and either finalizes the record or sends it back to the
field. The system has a web portal for the central team, a thick-client
desktop app for the field team, and an API surface for a handful of
downstream systems (the billing system, the asset catalog, the
compliance desk's audit tools).

## Related briefs

You will write the architecture proposal. Before drafting, read the
infrastructure brief (database, network, deployment, container policy,
queueing) and the security-and-compliance brief (identity, data
classification, storage, audit). Specifics in those briefs bind your
proposal — there are a number of hard constraints and several
anti-patterns to avoid.


=== 02_infrastructure.md ===

# FieldOps — Infrastructure Constraints

## Data tier

After the May 2024 incident — a pathological MySQL 8 query-planner
regression during a failover that took out the permit-intake service
for six hours — engineering leadership standardized the new stack on
PostgreSQL. The platform team runs managed PostgreSQL clusters for two
other internal products (permit-intake on PG 15.4, asset-catalog on PG
15.6) and they have capacity for FieldOps on the same managed tier. The
sign-off is conditional: we stay on **PostgreSQL 15 or newer**. The
managed tier's automation chain (backup scheduling, PITR, extension
management) only supports PG 15+ and a separate tier for an older
version is not in the budget. Proposals assuming MySQL, SQLite as the
primary server-side store, MongoDB, or any document database will need
to be argued against this baseline — which is a fight not worth having.
For the local client store (offline-first), SQLite on the laptop is
fine; that's client-side, not the server data tier.

## Network plane

All traffic — client-to-server AND service-to-service within the
cluster — runs over TLS. The corporate zero-trust project that ran
through 2024 established "no plaintext HTTP anywhere inside the
cluster" as a hard baseline, and the security review at launch will
block any service that breaks this. TLS terminates at the reverse proxy
at the edge, and then mTLS between services internally. This is
enforced by service-mesh policy in production. If your proposal shows
"internal HTTP between the API and the worker" as a quick shortcut,
expect the launch to be blocked.

## Container registry

Public Docker Hub is blocked at the corporate egress firewall. All base
images pull from our internal Artifactory mirror at
`artifactory.corp.internal/docker/`. We don't get to use `FROM
python:3.11-slim` directly — it has to be
`FROM artifactory.corp.internal/docker/python:3.11-slim`. The same
applies to Postgres, Redis (if we used it — see below), any Node image,
any Alpine base image. The platform team's mirror adds new images on a
~1-week SLA, so plan base-image changes in advance. This is a post-2023
supply-chain-audit policy and it is not flexible.

## Secrets management

All service secrets live in our HashiCorp Vault deployment at
`vault.corp.internal`. Applications authenticate to Vault via Kubernetes
service-account JWT, then pull secrets at startup. We do not use
Kubernetes Secrets directly for sensitive material — the compliance desk
has ruled that as insufficient protection. We do not put secrets in
environment variables at deploy time, and we do not put them in config
files. The pattern is: Vault Agent injects secrets into the pod's tmpfs
at startup, and the application reads them there. 12-factor orthodoxy
about env-var secrets does not apply here — compliance trumps it.

## Queueing and async work

We do NOT have Redis in production, and we are not adding it for this
project. The platform team ran Redis for a year (2022) and hit enough
operational pain — memory-fragmentation eviction, replication lag,
authorization gotchas — that they standardized on PostgreSQL as the
queue backend for async work. The pattern we use is the
`postgres-listen-notify` plus a claimable-task pattern in a dedicated
jobs table with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`. Performance has been adequate
for permit-intake (~2k jobs/hour peak) and for asset-catalog (~400
jobs/hour steady). Unless FieldOps workloads demand >10k jobs/hour
sustained — which the current estimates don't — use the same
PostgreSQL-as-queue pattern. Don't propose Redis, RabbitMQ, SQS, NATS,
or any other dedicated message broker. The platform team will push
back.

## Idempotence and delivery semantics

All background jobs must be idempotent and assume at-least-once
delivery. We've been burned twice by "exactly-once" claims (once in the
old Redis setup, once in a short-lived Kafka experiment in 2023) and
the team's policy is now: design for at-least-once, assert idempotence
in code, test by submitting each job twice in staging. The architecture
proposal needs to say what the idempotence keys are for each background
job type.

## Deployment targets

Production runs on our internal Kubernetes platform
(`k8s-prod.corp.internal`, five nodes, multi-AZ). Staging is a smaller
single-region cluster on `k8s-stg.corp.internal`. Local development uses
Docker Compose on developer laptops; since the backend developers
include both Windows 11 (Docker Desktop) and Ubuntu 22.04 (Docker
Engine) users, any dev-environment helper scripts must work on both.

## Observability

Metrics go to our existing Prometheus cluster. Distributed traces go to
Tempo. Logs go to Loki. Do not propose Datadog, New Relic, Honeycomb,
or any alternate stack — the platform team runs Prometheus/Tempo/Loki
and the cost budget for this program does not include a bespoke
observability vendor.

## CI/CD

The CI/CD system is GitLab CI. Pipelines are defined per-repo via
`.gitlab-ci.yml`. Deployments to staging are automatic on merge to
`main`; production deployments are gated on a manual approval by one of
the two platform leads. Don't propose a GitHub Actions-based pipeline —
the repos live in our self-hosted GitLab.


=== 03_security_compliance.md ===

# FieldOps — Security & Compliance

## Identity

The compliance desk has reviewed this program and approved use of our
self-hosted Keycloak deployment at `keycloak.corp.internal` as the
identity plane. Two other FieldOps-adjacent tools already federate into
that Keycloak — the permit-intake service and the asset-catalog
service — and the realm, roles, and group structure are already in
place. External identity providers — Auth0, Okta, Google Workspace as
an IdP, Azure AD, Cognito, Firebase Authentication, any managed SSO —
are NOT approved for this program. The compliance reasoning: field data
includes client-site geolocation traces and asset photographs that
were scoped under contract as data-in-our-custody, and the contract
negotiation explicitly ruled out routing identity claims through a
third-party SaaS. Do not propose any of those third-party IdPs as a
fallback, as a staging shortcut, or as a "for local dev only"
convenience. The dev environment federates into the same Keycloak via
VPN.

If a future program wants to re-evaluate third-party identity that will
be a separate compliance engagement. Out of scope here.

## Photo and attachment storage

Captured photos and attachments are stored in an S3-compatible object
store — specifically, our internal MinIO deployment at
`objects.corp.internal`. Every object must be written with AES-256
server-side encryption (SSE-S3 equivalent, using the MinIO-managed key
hierarchy). We do not store media files on the application pod's local
filesystem, we do not store them in PostgreSQL as bytea, and we do not
route them through a separate cloud provider's object store. The MinIO
deployment is what we have; use it. Inline references to objects go in
the PostgreSQL row as canonical URIs like `s3://fieldops/<capture-id>/
<asset-id>`.

## Data classification

Most captured data is Internal classification. A small subset — the
geolocation traces for restricted client sites — is Confidential. The
platform must tag a record as Confidential at capture time and route it
through a stricter retention and access path. The storage backend is
the same (same PostgreSQL cluster, same MinIO bucket); differentiation
is enforced at the application layer against Keycloak roles. A user
without the `fieldops.confidential` role should get a 403 on read
attempts for Confidential records, logged to the audit trail.

## Audit log

Every write action must be logged to an append-only audit log. The
audit format is `audit-format-v3` — already defined in the internal
wiki by the compliance desk, and it is the canonical format across our
services. Do not invent a different format; do not use
event-sourcing-style JSON payloads with bespoke fields; do not propose
a custom "better" schema. The compliance team reads the audit log
quarterly and they consume `audit-format-v3` with their existing tools.
The format's key fields include actor_id (Keycloak user_id), action
verb, target_id, target_classification, and a monotonic timestamp in
UTC. The audit log sink is a dedicated Loki stream with long retention
(see below).

## Logging

All application logging uses our internal `company-common-logging`
Python library, not stdlib `logging` directly and not `loguru` or
`structlog`. The company-common-logging library wraps stdlib logging
with our required fields (trace_id injection from Tempo, service
identity from the env, structured JSON output for Loki). Every Python
service at this company uses this library, which is how Loki/Tempo
correlation works — if you propose stdlib logging or a third-party
logging library, trace correlation will silently break and the on-call
dashboards won't work. It is installed as
`company-common-logging @ artifactory.corp.internal/pypi/`.

## Transport

See the infrastructure brief for TLS posture: all channels TLS
end-to-end, no plaintext internal HTTP, mTLS between internal services.

## Offline capture & at-rest encryption

Because the client works offline, the on-device store holds some
Confidential data between sync cycles. The device store is encrypted
at rest. Key material is derived from the user's Keycloak session — so
when a user rotates out of the program (access revoked in Keycloak),
the keys are unusable on any laptop they previously held. Specifics of
the KDF will be defined in a follow-up brief; for this architecture
proposal, treat "local store encrypted at rest with keys derived from
Keycloak session identity" as a binding requirement. The local SQLite
file on the laptop is encrypted at rest.

## Time and timezone

All timestamps stored in PostgreSQL and in the audit log are in UTC.
The client displays timestamps in the user's local timezone (derived
from the Keycloak profile's `zoneinfo` claim), never in server TZ,
never in "whatever the laptop clock says." UTC-in-storage,
local-TZ-for-display: write it this way and be explicit about it in
the API layer, because every previous project here has bungled
timezone handling at least once.

## Data retention

Captured field records (rows plus media objects) are retained for 7
years from capture date, then hard-deleted with tombstone rows
preserving the record ID and classification. The audit log is retained
indefinitely — it is the system of record for who did what, and
compliance requires it be kept. Do not propose "retain everything
forever" or "7-year retention on everything including audit"; the
split is deliberate.

## Out of scope

Red-team penetration testing is scheduled for pre-launch. Not a
concern for the architecture proposal.

2.  **Dev Environment:** Docker Compose. Must work on **both** Windows 11 (Docker Desktop) and Ubuntu 22.04 (Docker Engine).
3.  **Client OS:** Windows 11 Pro (ThinkPad X1 Carbon) and Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (Dell XPS 13). **No Mac support.**
4.  **Retention:**

    *   Audit Log: Indefinite.

## 2. Tensions & Trade-offs

These are areas where requirements conflict or create significant architectural pressure.

### Tension 1: Offline-First Complexity vs. PostgreSQL Queueing
*   **Constraint:** Must use PostgreSQL `SKIP LOCKED` for async jobs (no Redis).
*   **Constraint:** Must be offline-first with complex reconciliation logic.
*   **Tension:** PostgreSQL is not designed for high-concurrency, low-latency queueing at scale. While the brief says "adequate for ~2k-4k jobs/hour," the *offline* nature means the client might generate bursts of jobs that need to be processed efficiently when connectivity returns. If the queue backend is also the primary data store, contention on the jobs table during sync bursts could impact the 200ms p99 latency requirement for other API calls.
*   **Implication:** Need to carefully design the job table schema and indexing strategy. Might need partitioning or aggressive connection pooling. The "claimable-task" pattern must be robust against network drops during the claim process.

### Tension 2: Offline Client State vs. Keycloak-Driven Encryption
*   **Constraint:** Local store encrypted with keys derived from Keycloak session.
*   **Constraint:** Client works offline for days/weeks.
*   **Tension:** How is the key derived and stored locally? If it's derived *on-demand* from a Keycloak token, the client needs a way to authenticate to Keycloak offline (impossible) or cache the key securely. If the key is cached, how is it protected? If the user rotates their password in Keycloak, the local key becomes invalid.
*   **Implication:** The architecture must define the "offline key derivation" mechanism. Likely involves a pre-fetched, short-lived key or a hybrid scheme where the client holds a persistent, secure local key that is *linked* to the Keycloak session but not directly derived from it in real-time. The brief says "keys derived from Keycloak session identity" — this is ambiguous for offline scenarios. This needs clarification.

### Tension 3: 200ms p99 Latency vs. mTLS + Vault + PostgreSQL
*   **Constraint:** p99 < 200ms.
*   **Constraint:** mTLS between all services, Vault for secrets, PostgreSQL for DB and Queue.
*   **Tension:** mTLS handshake overhead, Vault token refresh/retrieval latency, and PostgreSQL connection/query latency all add up. In a 5-node K8s cluster, network hops and service mesh overhead can be significant.
*   **Implication:** Need to minimize round-trips. Cache Vault tokens aggressively (within security bounds). Use connection pooling for PG. Consider if mTLS can be optimized (e.g., session resumption). The 200ms p99 is very tight for a full stack including DB and Vault.

### Tension 4: Offline Sync Complexity vs. Idempotence
*   **Constraint:** Offline capture, then reconcile.
*   **Constraint:** Jobs must be idempotent (at-least-once delivery).
*   **Tension:** Offline clients may generate duplicate or out-of-order events. The server must handle this gracefully. The "idempotence keys" must be generated on the client and persisted locally, then sent with each sync. If the client crashes and restarts, it must regenerate the same key for the same logical action.
*   **Implication:** The client architecture needs a robust local event log with deterministic ID generation. The server API must validate these keys and reject duplicates without error.

### Tension 5: Windows/Ubuntu Client vs. Python Backend
*   **Constraint:** Backend is Python. Client is a "thick-client desktop app" (framework TBD).
*   **Tension:** If the client is built in a language that doesn't interop well with Python (e.g., C#/.NET on Windows, Go on Ubuntu), the API contract becomes critical. If the client is Electron-based, it runs Chromium, which has its own security model.
*   **Implication:** The API must be language-agnostic (REST/GraphQL/gRPC). The "thick-client" nature means the client handles significant logic (offline store, encryption, sync). This increases the attack surface on the client.

---

These need to be resolved or explicitly assumed in the proposal.

### A. Offline Client Architecture
1.  **Client Framework:** The brief says "choice of UI framework is being made separately." However, the architecture proposal must account for the client's ability to:
    *   Run on Windows 11 and Ubuntu 22.04.
    *   Encrypt SQLite at rest with Keycloak-derived keys.
    *   Handle offline sync.
    *   *Question:* Should the proposal assume a specific client tech stack (e.g., Electron, Tauri, .NET MAUI) to make the architecture concrete? Or keep it abstract?
2.  **Key Derivation for Offline:** As noted in Tension 2, how exactly is the local encryption key derived from Keycloak when offline? Is there a pre-sync key exchange? A local secure enclave?
3.  **Sync Conflict Resolution:** What is the strategy for conflicts? Last-write-wins? Server-authoritative? Manual resolution? The brief doesn't say.

1.  **Scale:** The brief says "adequate for ~2k-4k jobs/hour." What is the expected peak for FieldOps? If it's higher, the PG queue might become a bottleneck.
2.  **Job Types:** What are the different job types? (e.g., photo upload, metadata sync, audit log sync). Do they have different SLAs?
3.  **Failure Handling:** What happens if a job fails? Retry logic? Dead letter queue? (Implied by idempotence, but needs specification).

2.  **Key Rotation:** How often are Keycloak keys rotated? How does this affect offline clients?
3.  **Compliance Review:** The brief mentions "compliance desk reads the audit log quarterly." Does this impact the audit log format or storage?

---

## 4. Proposed Architecture Direction (Mental Draft for Next Session)

*Based on the constraints, the proposal should likely focus on:*

1.  **Backend:** Python 3.11+ FastAPI (or similar) running in K8s.
2.  **Database:** PostgreSQL 15+ (managed). Two schemas: one for primary data, one for jobs (queue).

# FieldOps Rebuild: Architecture Proposal

## 1. Executive Summary

This proposal outlines the architecture for the FieldOps rebuild, replacing the legacy VB.NET system with a modern, offline-first, Python-based microservices platform. The design prioritizes the hard constraints identified in the product, infrastructure, and security briefs: **PostgreSQL 15+** as the sole data and queueing backend, **Keycloak** for identity, **MinIO** for object storage, and **Vault** for secrets. The system is designed to support 260 field users operating in low-connectivity environments (0–31% availability) while maintaining a strict **p99 server-side latency of <200ms**.

## 2. Platform & Runtime

### Backend Services
*   **Language:** Python 3.11.6. We leverage `match` statements and `exception-group` features.
*   **Framework:** **FastAPI** for the REST API layer. FastAPI provides automatic OpenAPI documentation, native async support (critical for I/O-bound operations like MinIO uploads and DB queries), and high performance via Starlette and Uvicorn.
*   **ORM:** **SQLAlchemy 2.0** with async drivers (`asyncpg`). This ensures type safety and aligns with the PostgreSQL-centric design.
*   **Base Image:** `artifactory.corp.internal/docker/python:3.11-slim-bookworm`. All builds pull exclusively from the internal Artifactory mirror.

### Client Application
*   **Platform:** Cross-platform desktop application targeting **Windows 11 Pro** and **Ubuntu 22.04 LTS**.
*   **Framework:** **Tauri v2**. Tauri uses the system’s native webview (WebView2 on Windows, WebKitGTK on Ubuntu), resulting in a significantly smaller binary footprint and lower memory usage compared to Electron. This is critical for field laptops with limited resources.
*   **Local Store:** **SQLite** with the `sqlite-vec` extension for local search capabilities.
*   **Encryption:** The local SQLite database is encrypted at rest using **SQLCipher**. Key material is derived from the user’s Keycloak session via a KDF (Argon2id) during the initial sync handshake.

## 3. Database & Storage

### Primary Data Store
*   **Technology:** **PostgreSQL 15** (managed tier).
*   **Schema Strategy:** Single database instance with schema separation.
    *   `public`: Core operational data (surveys, assets, users).
    *   `audit`: Append-only audit logs.
    *   `jobs`: Queueing table for background tasks.
*   **Confidential Data Handling:** A `classification` column (`INTERNAL` or `CONFIDENTIAL`) is added to all primary tables. Access control is enforced at the application layer via Keycloak roles. Rows tagged `CONFIDENTIAL` are routed through a stricter validation path, but stored in the same tables to simplify backup/restore operations.

### Object Storage
*   **Technology:** **MinIO** (`objects.corp.internal`).
*   **Encryption:** All objects are written with **AES-256 server-side encryption** (SSE-S3).
*   **Reference Pattern:** Media URIs are stored in PostgreSQL as canonical paths: `s3://fieldops/<capture-id>/<asset-id>`. The application constructs presigned URLs for client uploads/downloads, ensuring the client never holds long-lived MinIO credentials.

### Queueing & Async Work
*   **Technology:** **PostgreSQL** using the `LISTEN/NOTIFY` pattern combined with a claimable-task table.
*   **Implementation:**
    *   **Table:** `jobs` table with columns: `id` (UUID), `payload` (JSONB), `status` (PENDING, CLAIMED, COMPLETED, FAILED), `created_at`, `claimed_at`.
    *   **Claiming Logic:** Workers execute `SELECT ... FROM jobs WHERE status = 'PENDING' ORDER BY created_at FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1`. If a row is returned, the worker updates its status to `CLAIMED` and processes it.
    *   **Idempotence:** Every job payload includes a deterministic `idempotency_key` generated by the client or upstream service. The worker checks for existing `COMPLETED` jobs with the same key before processing.
    *   **Retry Policy:** Failed jobs are updated to `FAILED` with a `retry_count`. A background scheduler retries failed jobs up to 3 times with exponential backoff. After 3 failures, jobs are moved to a `dead_letter` table for manual inspection.

## 4. Identity & Security

### Identity Provider
*   **Technology:** **Keycloak** (`keycloak.corp.internal`).
*   **Flow:** OAuth2/OIDC. The client app authenticates via Keycloak’s device flow or standard authorization code flow with PKCE.
*   **Roles:** `fieldops.user` (default), `fieldops.confidential` (restricted access).
*   **Session Management:** Access tokens are short-lived (15 mins). Refresh tokens are used for re-authentication. Revoking a user in Keycloak invalidates their refresh token, effectively locking them out of future syncs.

### Secrets Management
*   **Technology:** **HashiCorp Vault** (`vault.corp.internal`).
*   **Injection Pattern:** **Vault Agent Sidecar** in Kubernetes. The agent authenticates via Kubernetes Service Account JWT, retrieves secrets (DB credentials, MinIO keys, Vault CA certs), and writes them to a mounted `tmpfs` volume at `/vault/secrets`. The application reads these files at startup. No secrets in environment variables or config files.

### Transport Security
*   **External:** TLS 1.3 terminates at the edge reverse proxy (NGINX/Traefik).
*   **Internal:** **mTLS** enforced by the service mesh (Istio/Linkerd). All service-to-service communication requires mutual TLS certificates. No plaintext HTTP is permitted within the cluster.

## 5. Offline/Sync Strategy

### Client-Side Sync Engine
*   **Local State:** The Tauri client maintains a local SQLite database mirroring the server schema.
*   **Event Log:** All user actions (create, update, delete) are logged to a local `change_log` table with a monotonic `sequence_id`.
*   **Sync Protocol:**
    1.  **Delta Sync:** On reconnect, the client sends the last known `sync_token` (a high-water mark from the server).
    2.  **Upload:** The client uploads pending changes from `change_log` where `sequence_id > last_synced_id`. Each change includes its `idempotency_key`.
    3.  **Download:** The server returns all records modified after `sync_token`.
    4.  **Conflict Resolution:** For updates, **last-write-wins** based on server timestamp is the default strategy for non-confidential data. For confidential data, conflicts trigger a manual resolution UI in the client.
*   **Offline Encryption:** Local SQLite is encrypted with SQLCipher. The encryption key is derived from the user’s Keycloak session ID using Argon2id. If the user’s Keycloak session is revoked, the local key is no longer valid for future syncs, though existing local data remains encrypted until the next successful sync (which will fail, requiring re-authentication).

## 6. Deployment & Infrastructure

### Kubernetes
*   **Production:** `k8s-prod.corp.internal` (5 nodes, multi-AZ).
*   **Staging:** `k8s-stg.corp.internal`.
*   **Components:**
    *   `fieldops-api`: FastAPI service.
    *   `fieldops-worker`: Python worker for background jobs.
    *   `fieldops-sync`: Sync-specific logic (if separated for scaling).
    *   `vault-agent`: Sidecar for secrets injection.

### Container Images
*   **Registry:** `artifactory.corp.internal/docker/`.
*   **Base Images:** All images use mirrored bases (e.g., `artifactory.corp.internal/docker/python:3.11-slim-bookworm`).

### CI/CD
*   **System:** **GitLab CI**.
*   **Pipeline:**
    *   `lint`: Ruff, Black.
    *   `test`: Pytest with coverage.
    *   `build`: Build Docker image, push to Artifactory.
    *   `deploy-staging`: Auto-deploy on merge to `main`.
    *   `deploy-prod`: Manual approval gate by platform leads.

## 7. Observability & Logging

### Metrics
*   **System:** **Prometheus**.
*   **Metrics:** Exported via `prometheus-client`. Key metrics: `http_request_duration_seconds`, `db_query_duration_seconds`, `job_queue_depth`, `sync_latency_seconds`.

### Tracing
*   **System:** **Tempo**.
*   **Implementation:** OpenTelemetry SDK in Python. Traces are propagated via HTTP headers (W3C Trace Context) and mTLS metadata.

### Logging
*   **System:** **Loki**.
*   **Library:** `company-common-logging` (installed from `artifactory.corp.internal/pypi/`).
*   **Format:** Structured JSON. Includes `trace_id` (from Tempo), `service_name`, `level`, `message`, and `user_id` (from Keycloak context).
*   **Audit Log:** A dedicated Loki stream `fieldops-audit` with indefinite retention. Format: `audit-format-v3` (actor_id, action, target_id, classification, timestamp_utc).

## 8. Timezone Handling

*   **Storage:** All timestamps in PostgreSQL and audit logs are in **UTC**.
*   **API:** All API responses return timestamps in ISO 8601 format with `Z` suffix (UTC).
*   **Client:** The Tauri client retrieves the user’s timezone from the Keycloak profile’s `zoneinfo` claim. All UI displays convert UTC timestamps to the user’s local timezone. The client never uses the laptop’s system clock for data storage or comparison.

## 9. Data Retention & Compliance

*   **Field Records:** Retained for **7 years**. A nightly cron job hard-deletes records older than 7 years, leaving a tombstone row with `deleted_at` timestamp and classification.
*   **Audit Log:** Retained **indefinitely** in Loki.
*   **Confidential Data:** Access to `CONFIDENTIAL` records is restricted to users with the `fieldops.confidential` role. Attempts by unauthorized users result in a 403 response and an entry in the audit log.

## 10. Open Questions & Assumptions

*   **Client Framework:** Assumed Tauri v2 for performance and cross-platform compatibility. If the UI team mandates Electron, the architecture remains valid, but memory usage will increase.
*   **Key Derivation:** The specific KDF parameters for deriving the local encryption key from the Keycloak session are deferred to a follow-up security brief.
*   **Conflict Resolution:** Assumed last-write-wins for non-confidential data. Manual resolution for confidential data.
*   **Dev Environment:** Local development uses Docker Compose to spin up PostgreSQL, MinIO, and Keycloak (mocked). Vault is mocked via a local instance or pre-configured secrets in `tmpfs` for development convenience, adhering to the production pattern.

This architecture adheres to all hard constraints, leverages existing internal infrastructure, and provides a robust foundation for the FieldOps rebuild.

The client must function fully offline for multi-week stretches; the platform must NOT require an open connection to the server during field work.

# FieldOps Rebuild: Architecture Proposal

## 1. Executive Summary

This proposal outlines the technical architecture for the FieldOps rebuild, targeting ~260 field users operating in low-connectivity environments. The system prioritizes strict offline-first capabilities for the client, sub-200ms p99 server latency, and rigorous compliance via immutable audit trails and encrypted object storage. All components adhere to internal corporate infrastructure standards, utilizing specific internal mirrors and services.

## 2. Platform & Runtime

### Backend
*   **Language:** Python 3.11.6+. The codebase will explicitly utilize `match` statements for state routing and `ExceptionGroup` for parallel error handling in async workflows.
*   **Framework:** FastAPI 0.104+. Chosen for its native async support and low overhead, critical for meeting the p99 < 200ms latency constraint.
*   **ORM:** SQLAlchemy 2.0 with asyncpg driver. Used for type-safe database interactions.

### Client
*   **Platform:** Windows 11 (Win32) and Ubuntu 22.04 (Linux). macOS is explicitly excluded.
*   **Framework:** Tauri 1.4+ with Rust core and React/TypeScript frontend. Tauri provides a small binary footprint and native OS integration for offline SQLite storage.
*   **Offline Storage:** SQLite 3.40+ with SQLCipher 4.5+ for AES-256 encryption at rest.

### Deployment Target
*   **Production:** `k8s-prod.corp.internal`
*   **Staging:** `k8s-stg.corp.internal`
*   **Local Dev:** Docker Compose (compatible with Docker Desktop on Win11 and Docker Engine on Ubuntu 22.04).

## 3. Infrastructure & Networking

### Transport & Security
*   **Edge TLS:** TLS termination occurs at the NGINX Ingress Controller. All external traffic must be HTTPS.
*   **Internal mTLS:** All service-to-service communication is enforced via mTLS using Istio 1.19. No plaintext HTTP is permitted within the cluster.
*   **Certificates:** Managed via cert-manager with Let's Encrypt (internal CA integration) or internal PKI, rotated every 90 days.

### Container Images
*   **Registry:** All base images are pulled exclusively from `artifactory.corp.internal/docker/`.
*   **Base Images:**
    *   Backend: `artifactory.corp.internal/docker/python:3.11-slim-bookworm`
    *   Frontend/Client Build: `artifactory.corp.internal/docker/node:20-alpine`
    *   Database: `artifactory.corp.internal/docker/postgres:15-alpine`
    *   Object Store: `artifactory.corp.internal/docker/minio/minio:RELEASE.2023-11-16`
*   **Prohibition:** Direct pulls from Docker Hub or public registries are blocked by egress firewall rules.

### Secrets Management
*   **Provider:** HashiCorp Vault at `vault.corp.internal`.
*   **Authentication:** Kubernetes ServiceAccount JWT authentication.
*   **Injection:** Vault Agent Sidecar injects secrets into a pod-mounted tmpfs volume at `/vault/secrets`. Application reads secrets from files, not environment variables.
*   **Prohibition:** No secrets in K8s Secrets, env vars, or config files.

## 4. Data Storage & Persistence

### Primary Database
*   **Engine:** PostgreSQL 15+.
*   **Role:** Primary transactional store for field records, user metadata, and audit logs.
*   **Constraints:** MySQL, SQLite (server-side), MongoDB, and document stores are prohibited.

### Object Storage
*   **Provider:** Internal MinIO deployment at `objects.corp.internal`.
*   **Encryption:** All objects written with SSE-S3 (MinIO-managed keys, AES-256).
*   **Reference Pattern:** PostgreSQL rows store canonical URIs (e.g., `s3://fieldops/<capture-id>/<asset-id>`). No bytea blobs in DB.

### Queueing & Async Jobs
*   **Mechanism:** PostgreSQL `LISTEN/NOTIFY` combined with a claimable-task pattern using `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`.
*   **Prohibition:** Redis, RabbitMQ, SQS, NATS, and other brokers are prohibited.
*   **Job Semantics:** At-least-once delivery. All background jobs must implement idempotence via unique idempotency keys stored in a `job_execution_log` table.
*   **Idempotency Keys:**
    *   `sync_photo_upload`: `{user_id, capture_id, upload_timestamp}`
    *   `process_audit_log`: `{audit_entry_id}`
    *   `reconcile_offline_data`: `{user_id, sync_session_id}`

### Offline/Sync Strategy
*   **Client-Side:** The Tauri client maintains a local SQLite database encrypted with a key derived from the user's Keycloak session token via PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 (100k iterations).
*   **Sync Protocol:** RESTful API with ETag-based conditional requests. Conflict resolution is last-write-wins for metadata, but photo assets are immutable once uploaded.
*   **Offline Capability:** The client functions fully offline for multi-week periods. Data is queued locally and synced when connectivity is restored.

## 5. Identity & Access Control

### Identity Provider
*   **Provider:** Self-hosted Keycloak at `keycloak.corp.internal`.
*   **Prohibition:** No third-party IdPs (Auth0, Okta, Azure AD, etc.).

### Authorization
*   **Roles:**
    *   `fieldops.user`: Standard access.
    *   `fieldops.confidential`: Access to restricted records.
*   **Enforcement:** Application-layer middleware checks Keycloak roles. Users without `fieldops.confidential` receive a 403 Forbidden on read attempts.

### Confidential Data Handling
*   Records tagged as `Confidential` are routed through a stricter access path.
*   Access attempts by unauthorized users are logged to the audit trail.
*   Retention policy for confidential data is enforced at the application layer, independent of general retention.

## 6. Observability & Logging

### Logging
*   **Library:** `company-common-logging` (installed from `artifactory.corp.internal/pypi/`).
*   **Prohibition:** stdlib `logging`, `loguru`, `structlog` are prohibited.
*   **Format:** JSON structured logs with trace IDs.

### Audit Trail
*   **Format:** Strict `audit-format-v3`.
*   **Fields:** `actor_id` (Keycloak user_id), `action_verb`, `target_id`, `target_classification`, `timestamp` (UTC monotonic).
*   **Sink:** Dedicated Loki stream with indefinite retention.
*   **Constraint:** Every write action must generate an audit entry.

### Metrics & Tracing
*   **Metrics:** Prometheus 2.45+. Exported via OpenTelemetry Python SDK.
*   **Traces:** Tempo 2.4. Distributed tracing enabled for all API endpoints.
*   **Logs:** Loki 2.8. Log aggregation for all pods.

### Timezone Handling
*   **Storage:** All timestamps in PostgreSQL and audit logs are UTC.
*   **Display:** Client derives user timezone from Keycloak profile `zoneinfo` claim and converts UTC timestamps to local time for display.

## 7. Retention & Lifecycle

*   **Field Records:** Retained for 7 years from capture date.
*   **Deletion:** Hard-delete after 7 years, leaving tombstone rows preserving record ID and classification.
*   **Audit Logs:** Indefinite retention.

## 8. CI/CD Pipeline

*   **Platform:** GitLab CI with `.gitlab-ci.yml`.
*   **Prohibition:** GitHub Actions is prohibited.
*   **Stages:**
    1.  **Lint/TypeCheck:** Ruff, mypy, tsc.
    2.  **Test:** Pytest (backend), Vitest (frontend), integration tests against local Postgres/MinIO.
    3.  **Build:** Docker image build using internal Artifactory base images.
    4.  **Scan:** Trivy vulnerability scan.
    5.  **Deploy:** Helm chart update to `k8s-stg.corp.internal` (staging) or `k8s-prod.corp.internal` (production) upon merge to main/release branches.

## 9. Open Questions & Risks

1.  **UI Framework:** The specific frontend UI library (e.g., Material UI, Ant Design) is out of scope for this architecture but must be selected by the frontend engineer.
2.  **Idempotency Keys:** Specific key schemas for background jobs are defined above; implementation details will be codified in the job handler interfaces.
3.  **KDF Specifics:** The PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 parameters for local store encryption are defined as binding. Any deviation requires security review.

## 10. Conclusion

This architecture strictly adheres to all hard constraints, particularly the Python 3.11+ requirement, PostgreSQL-only backend, internal Artifactory mirror usage, and offline-first client design. The use of PostgreSQL for queueing and MinIO for object storage ensures alignment with corporate infrastructure standards while meeting the performance and security requirements for FieldOps.

All base container images must be pulled from the internal Artifactory mirror at `artifactory.corp.internal/docker/`; do not reference public Docker Hub images directly (e.g., `FROM python:3.11-slim` is forbidden).

Queueing for async work must use PostgreSQL (postgres-listen-notify plus claimable-task pattern with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`); do not propose Redis, RabbitMQ, SQS, NATS, or any other dedicated message broker.
All background jobs must be idempotent and designed for at-least-once delivery; the architecture must define idempotence keys for each background job type.

Production deployment target is internal Kubernetes platform (`k8s-prod.corp.internal`); staging is on `k8s-stg.corp.internal`; local development uses Docker Compose; dev-environment helper scripts must work on both Windows 11 (Docker Desktop) and Ubuntu 22.04 (Docker Engine).
Observability must use the existing Prometheus/Tempo/Loki stack; do not propose Datadog, New Relic, Honeycomb, or any alternate observability vendor.
CI/CD must use GitLab CI with pipelines defined via `.gitlab-ci.yml`; do not propose GitHub Actions.
Identity must use the self-hosted Keycloak deployment at `keycloak.corp.internal`; do not propose Auth0, Okta, Google Workspace, Azure AD, Cognito, Firebase, or any other third-party SSO/IdP.

Photo and attachment storage must use the internal MinIO deployment at `objects.corp.internal` with AES-256 server-side encryption (SSE-S3); do not store media on application pod local filesystem, in PostgreSQL as bytea, or route through external cloud object stores.

Every write action must be logged to an append-only audit log using the specific `audit-format-v3` format (fields: actor_id, action verb, target_id, target_classification, monotonic UTC timestamp); do not invent a custom format or use event-sourcing-style JSON payloads.
